title: Practice Test 3: Claude Certified Architect Foundations
description:
60 unique scenario-based questions with another random selection of 4 out of 6 scenarios. Domain distribution matches official exam guide weightings. Topics include agentic loop implementation, MCP tool design, Claude Code configuration, structured output, and context window management.

As with the real exam, every question begins with a randomly selected scenario to frame it. These scenarios repeat, and that is expected.

Every question has been validated for technical accuracy and topic scope compliance. Detailed explanations with documentation references follow each question.

Prerequisite: Review the official exam guide and complete Anthropic's free certification preparation courses (or have equivalent hands-on experience).

prompt.question:
SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

QUESTION: One engineer on this team is prototyping a mock_refund_ledger MCP server to exercise refund edge cases. It is unstable, must stay out of the repository, and should be available only to that engineer across their local projects. Where should it be configured?
answers: Declare it in "~/.claude/settings.json", the user settings file that governs Claude Code behavior.
Register it in the user-scoped "~/.claude.json" file so it stays private to that engineer's machine.
Add it to the project's ".mcp.json" file so it is shared with everyone who pulls the repository.
Document the server's tools in the project CLAUDE.md so the agent knows which calls are available.
feedbacks: The ~/.claude/settings.json file holds user settings such as permissions and behavior configuration. It does not hold MCP server definitions. Claude Code writes MCP server registrations for personal scopes to a separate file, ~/.claude.json, which it maintains for itself.

User-scoped MCP servers are stored in ~/.claude.json. This file is never committed to version control, and the servers in it are available in every project on that machine for that user account. This matches a personal, experimental server that should be available to one engineer in all of their projects without reaching teammates.

The .mcp.json file at the project root is how a team shares MCP servers, and it is meant to be checked into version control. Teammates who pull it are asked to approve the server before it is used. Placing an unstable personal prototype there would expose it to the whole team, which is what the engineer wants to avoid.

CLAUDE.md supplies project instructions and context. It does not connect an MCP server or make its tools callable. A description there would also be committed to the repository and shared with the whole team, which is the opposite of the stated goal.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code separates MCP servers by scope. The scope decides who sees the server and whether it is stored in the repository. Project scope writes a .mcp.json file at the project root that is meant to be committed. Every contributor who pulls the repo is then offered the same backend tools once they approve the server in an interactive session. Secrets are injected through environment variable substitution, such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}, rather than committed as values. User scope instead writes the server into ~/.claude.json. This is a per-machine file that is never part of the repository, and it makes the server available across all of that user's projects. There is also a local scope, which is the default for claude mcp add. It is stored in the same ~/.claude.json file but is tied to a single project path. It is the right choice when a private server should apply to only one checkout. The engineer wants the mock refund ledger to be available in all of their projects while staying private, so user scope (for example claude mcp add --scope user) is the right fit.

The location of the config file defines who the server is shared with. Anything in .mcp.json is shared team configuration, and teammates are asked to approve it before use. Anything in ~/.claude.json is personal state that Claude Code manages for the individual account. This is why experimental or unstable servers belong in the personal file. The engineer can change them freely without breaking anyone else's sessions or adding clutter to version control. When the same server name exists in more than one scope, Claude Code does not merge the entries. It uses the whole entry from the highest-precedence scope, in the order local, then project, then user. So a user-scoped server never overrides a project-scoped team server with the same name. Only a local-scope entry comes before the project entry in that order. If a team server with the same name already exists, give the personal prototype a different name.

The other options confuse nearby files and mechanisms. ~/.claude/settings.json is a real file, but it holds user settings such as permissions and hooks, not MCP server registrations. The settings documentation clearly separates it from ~/.claude.json. CLAUDE.md is project context that is always loaded. It cannot connect to a server, and it is committed to the repository anyway. Committing the prototype to .mcp.json would work technically, but it breaks the privacy requirement. It would share an unstable server with the whole team, and they would then be asked to approve it.

See Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP for scope definitions and precedence, and Claude Code settings for the difference between ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.claude.json.

QUESTION: The agent extracts charge amounts, order numbers, and dispute reasons from billing emails and outputs a confidence value for each field. Overall accuracy on a labeled validation set is 97%, so the team plans to stop reviewing high-confidence outputs. What should they do first?
answers: Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to assign lower confidence when uncertain.
Have a second model call re-rate each extraction's confidence and trust the agreed values.
Measure accuracy separately by request type and by field, and automate only segments with stable results.
Raise the automation threshold to a stricter confidence cutoff across every field before removing any review.
feedbacks: Prompt wording does not make a model-generated confidence value calibrated. The model can still be confident and wrong on hard cases. Only measurement against labeled data tells you how the score relates to real accuracy in each segment.
Agreement between two self-ratings is still a self-rating. It is not evidence about actual error rates. It adds cost and latency, and it still does not answer how accurate each segment is.

An overall figure of 97% can hide a field or request type where accuracy is much lower, such as dispute reasons in forwarded email threads. Breaking the labeled set down by segment shows where high confidence really matches correct values. Review is then removed only where the data supports it.

A single stricter cutoff assumes the confidence value means the same thing for every field, and calibration data rarely supports that. It reduces the share of automated outputs, but it does not show whether a specific field or request type is failing behind the overall number.
prompt.explanation:
A confidence value in a structured output is just another field that the model fills in. Anthropic's structured outputs documentation includes a classification example whose schema has a confidence field. The same mechanism lets an extraction schema ask for one. But a schema guarantees only the shape and type of the JSON. Nothing in the API turns that number into a calibrated probability of being correct, and the documentation does not describe it as one. A confidence score is a hint produced by the model, and you must find out what it really means by testing. You do this by comparing the model's outputs against labeled examples and checking how often a given confidence level is actually right.

The trap in this scenario is the aggregate metric, a single number that combines all the results. An overall accuracy of 97% across three fields and several request types can easily hide one segment where accuracy is much lower while the model still reports high confidence. An example is dispute reasons extracted from forwarded email threads. If the team removes human review based only on the overall number, those errors go straight into refund decisions and escalation summaries. The careful approach is to split the labeled validation set by field and by request type. The team should confirm that performance is stable in each segment and reduce review only where the evidence supports it. Anthropic's evaluation guidance says the same thing. Use task-specific evaluations built from labeled data that matches the real-world distribution, and include edge cases. Choose metrics such as precision and recall that match the production goal, rather than relying on one overall number.

Each of the other approaches misses this. Raising the cutoff for every field treats the confidence score as if it behaved the same way across fields. It reduces automation coverage without showing where the real weakness is. Asking the model in the prompt to be more conservative changes wording, not the actual relationship between the score and correctness. A model that is already confident and wrong on hard cases does not become reliable because it was told to be modest. A second model call that re-rates confidence is still a self-assessment, so agreement between two unvalidated ratings gives no real evidence of which values are correct. After the team verifies accuracy for each segment and sets review thresholds for each field, it should keep sampling the automated outputs from each segment (stratified sampling). This is how the team catches new error patterns that appear after the review load drops.

See Structured outputs for how schema-constrained fields such as a confidence value are produced, and Create strong empirical evaluations for building labeled test sets that match the real distribution and choosing metrics that reflect the production routing decision.

QUESTION: Order-status questions always resolve with get_customer followed by lookup_order, and the team wants those answers consistent and inexpensive, while returns and billing disputes vary widely in the steps required. How should the team structure these two kinds of work?
answers: Run status questions through a predefined code path that calls the two tools in order, and keep the model-driven loop for returns and disputes.
Set "max_turns" to two for status questions so the agent loop is forced to stop once the lookup_order result has been returned.
Build a hard-coded decision tree covering every request category so that each tool sequence is predictable and reviewable before deployment.
Keep every request inside the model-driven loop and add a system prompt rule instructing Claude to call the two tools in order for status questions.
feedbacks: Anthropic's guidance separates workflows, where code follows predefined paths, from agents, where Claude directs its own tool usage based on context. A status check has a known, fixed sequence, so a workflow gives consistency and lower cost. Returns and disputes are ambiguous, so they still need Claude to decide the next tool based on what each result shows.

The turn cap is a safety limit on tool-use round trips. It is not a way to set which tools run or in what order. Reaching the cap ends the run with an error result subtype instead of a normal completion, so it cannot be the mechanism that makes status checks consistent.

Returns and billing disputes vary in the steps they need. This is the situation where a fixed decision tree fails and the model needs to choose the next tool based on intermediate results. Removing model-driven selection for the ambiguous cases would lower first-contact resolution, not improve it.

A prompt rule only makes it more likely that Claude follows the sequence. It does not make the path fixed, and the loop still pays for reasoning on every turn. When the steps are fully known in advance, a predefined code path gives the predictability and savings the team wants.
prompt.explanation:
Anthropic makes a clear distinction between two ways of organizing LLM-powered systems. In a workflow, your code follows predefined paths. It decides which calls happen and in what order, and the model provides the reasoning or language at each step. In an agent, the model dynamically directs its own process. On every turn it looks at the request, the tool descriptions, and the results already in context. Then it decides whether to call a tool, which one to call, or whether to answer directly. Workflows give predictability and consistency on well-defined tasks. Agents give flexibility on tasks where the steps cannot be known ahead of time. See Building effective agents.

Technically, the agent side is a loop based on stop_reason. Your application defines what the model can use (the MCP tools and their schemas). Claude sends a tool_use request, your harness runs it and adds a tool_result, and the loop repeats while the model keeps asking for tools. Nothing in that loop fixes the order of calls. The model makes each next decision again from the history collected so far. This is why a system prompt rule about tool order can only make a sequence likely, not guaranteed. It is also why the loop still costs a reasoning round trip for each step. This contract is described in How tool use works.

The scenario contains both kinds of task. An order-status check is a standard example of a workflow. The two tool calls are always the same, so a short code path can run them directly and pass the results to the model to write a reply. This gives the same behavior every time at lower cost. Returns and billing disputes are the opposite. Whether a second lookup, a partial refund, or an escalation comes next depends on what the earlier results show, so the model-driven loop is the right choice. The question tests whether you choose the pattern for each task type, rather than using one pattern for everything.

Each of the remaining approaches uses a mechanism in the wrong way. A hard-coded decision tree for every category removes the model's ability to adapt in the cases where the requests are ambiguous. A low max_turns value is a limit on tool-use round trips in the Claude Agent SDK. Reaching it ends the run with an error_max_turns result instead of a normal completion. It says nothing about which tool runs, so it is a safety limit, not a workflow. The loop and its limits are documented in Agent loop.

QUESTION: This team is adding a billing-dispute investigation subagent through an AgentDefinition. The subagent must gather evidence but never issue refunds, and the coordinator must delegate to it reliably. Which two configuration choices accomplish this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Set the subagent's "tools" allowlist to "get_customer" and "lookup_order" so "process_refund" is absent from its session.
State in the subagent's "prompt" that it must never call "process_refund" and leave "tools" unset so it inherits every tool.
Omit the "description" field because the coordinator already supplies the dispute details in the prompt it passes when spawning the subagent.
Write a "description" stating exactly when billing-dispute investigation should be delegated, since the coordinator decides delegation from it.
feedbacks: The tools field is an allowlist. When it is present, the subagent receives only the listed tools, and any tool left out is not part of its session at all. This makes the refund restriction a structural guarantee instead of an instruction the model might ignore. That is the right standard for a financial action.

Leaving out tools gives the subagent every tool available to subagents, including process_refund. The prompt instruction is then the only thing that stops the subagent from issuing a refund. Prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance, meaning the model is not guaranteed to follow them. That is not enough when the action has direct financial consequences and a deterministic restriction is available.

The description and prompt are both required fields of an AgentDefinition, and they have different purposes. The prompt the coordinator passes when it spawns the subagent carries task details. But the description is what Claude reads to decide whether to delegate at all, so leaving it out makes routing unreliable.

Claude decides whether to invoke a subagent by matching the task against each subagent's description. A vague or generic description leads to unreliable delegation. A clear description of when to use this subagent is how the coordinator learns to route billing disputes to it consistently.
prompt.explanation:
An AgentDefinition in the Claude Agent SDK has two required fields and a small set of optional ones, and each field has a separate job. The parent agent reads the description to decide whether to delegate. Claude compares the current task against every subagent's description and picks the one that fits, so this field in effect defines the routing. The prompt is the subagent's own system prompt. It defines the subagent's role and behavior after it has been chosen. Mixing up the two is a common mistake. A detailed prompt does not help routing if the description does not say when the subagent applies.

The optional tools field is an allowlist. If you set it, the subagent gets only those tools and nothing else. If you leave it out, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents. A tool missing from the allowlist is not present in the subagent's session at all. The model works without it, instead of getting a permission prompt or a tool error. That is why limiting a billing-investigation subagent to get_customer and lookup_order is a structural guarantee. process_refund cannot be called because it does not exist in that context. A sentence in the system prompt saying "never issue refunds" is a reasonable addition. But on its own it gives only probabilistic compliance, and the exam consistently treats prompt-only enforcement of financial actions as an anti-pattern. (Note that the allowlist controls which tools exist. A rule about refund amounts for a subagent that is allowed to refund would need a PreToolUse hook instead.) There is also a separate disallowedTools list for removing tools, including MCP server-level patterns. It is useful when removing a few tools from the inherited set is easier than listing all the allowed ones.

A subagent is a fresh, isolated agent instance. A non-fork subagent does not receive the parent's conversation history, tool results, or parent system prompt. It receives its own prompt, the task text passed when it is spawned, the project CLAUDE.md, and its tool definitions. So designing the definition means answering three questions clearly. When should this agent be chosen (description)? How should it behave (prompt)? What is it technically able to do (tools)? The docs show a read-only analysis pattern built from Read, Grep, and Glob. That is the same idea applied to code. In this scenario, the read-only set is the two lookup tools.

See Subagents in the SDK for the AgentDefinition fields, tool restriction behavior, and what subagents inherit, and Create custom subagents for how Claude uses descriptions to decide when to delegate.

QUESTION: After many turns untangling a billing dispute across three orders, the main agent delegates drafting the final resolution to a specialized subagent that must work from the complete conversation so far. Which delegation approach achieves this?
answers: Pass the main agent's session ID in the delegation prompt so the subagent resumes that conversation itself.
Spawn the drafting subagent as a fork so it starts with a copy of the main agent's conversation so far.
Trigger context compaction in the main agent first so the resulting summary carries over into the new subagent.
Spawn a standard subagent and rely on it sharing the main agent's session history automatically.
feedbacks: No mechanism lets a subagent attach to its parent's session by reading an identifier from its prompt. Resuming applies to a subagent that was spawned earlier and kept its own history. It does not let a subagent take over the parent's history. The session ID would arrive as plain text in an otherwise empty context.

A forked subagent is the documented exception to context isolation. Instead of starting fresh, it copies the parent conversation up to the point of the fork. That gives the drafting subagent every turn of the dispute word for word, which is what the goal requires.

Compaction changes what the main agent itself holds in context. It does not change what a new subagent receives. A non-fork subagent still starts fresh with only its own system prompt and the delegation prompt. Compaction also replaces the full conversation with a summary, so it does not meet the stated goal.

A standard (non-fork) subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It does not see the parent's conversation history or earlier tool results, even though it runs inside the same session. The only content passed from parent to subagent is the delegation prompt. So relying on automatic sharing leaves the subagent with none of the dispute's history.
prompt.explanation:
In every Agent SDK design, remember that a subagent is a separate agent instance, not a thread inside the main agent's conversation. The main agent calls the Agent tool (the Task tool in older versions) to start a subagent. A standard subagent starts with a fresh context window. It receives its own system prompt from its AgentDefinition, the delegation prompt, and environment details such as CLAUDE.md files. It does not receive the parent's system prompt, the parent's conversation history, or any tool results the parent has already collected. In the same way, the subagent's own intermediate tool calls stay inside it, and only its final message returns to the parent. This isolation is deliberate. It keeps the main conversation's context budget intact. It lets many subagents run in parallel without interfering with each other. And it lets each subagent have specialized instructions that would only add noise to the main prompt.

The documented exception is the fork. A forked subagent copies the conversation so far instead of starting empty. So it begins with the same twenty or so turns of dispute history that the main agent has collected. In current Claude Code and SDK versions, Claude can start a fork by invoking the Agent tool with subagent_type: "fork". An application can deny forks through permissions if it does not want them. A fork has real costs. It gives up the benefit of context isolation, and it carries the full token cost of the parent conversation. So it is the right choice only when the subtask really needs the complete history rather than a selected summary. For most delegations, the usual pattern is to write the relevant facts directly into the delegation prompt, which is cheaper and good enough. In this scenario, the stated requirement for the complete conversation is what makes forking the correct choice.

The other approaches misunderstand where a subagent's context comes from. Assuming a standard subagent shares the session history confuses being in the same session with inheriting its conversation. Nothing passes from parent to subagent except the prompt string. Compacting the main agent first only changes the main agent's own context. The subagent still gets nothing beyond the delegation prompt, and the history is also reduced to a summary. Passing a session ID in the prompt relies on a resume mechanism that does not exist for a subagent taking over its parent's conversation. Resuming is a way to continue a subagent that was spawned earlier, with its own saved history. It is not a way to import the parent's history.

See Subagents in the SDK for the inheritance table and fork behavior, and Create custom subagents for how Claude Code builds a subagent's starting context.

QUESTION: Yesterday's Claude Code session audited the escalation logic across this agent's repository. Since then a teammate changed two policy files and committed them with git, outside of Claude Code. Which two approaches let today's work continue without full re-exploration? (Select TWO.)
answers: Start a fresh session and have Claude re-explore the entire repository so no stale findings carry over.
Resume the session and reference the two rewritten files with "@" so Claude re-reads their current contents before continuing.
Start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of yesterday's findings and the names of the two rewritten files.
Resume the session with "claude --continue" and proceed, since resumption reloads the latest contents of every previously read file.
feedbacks: Only two files changed. Throwing away all of yesterday's findings and exploring the whole repository again wastes tokens and time. It also fills the context window again with reads that were still valid. The guidance for resumed work is to point Claude at the specific changes instead of asking for broad re-exploration.

A resumed session restores earlier messages, tool calls, and tool results as they were. So the two files still appear in context with yesterday's contents. Referencing them with an at-sign (@) makes Claude read the files from disk before it responds. This replaces only the out-of-date parts and keeps the rest of the audit intact.

When stored tool results are known to be out of date, a documented alternative to resuming is a new session that is given a short, structured summary of earlier findings plus the names of the changed files. Claude keeps the conclusions and re-reads only the files that were named. It never holds outdated file contents in its context.

Resuming restores the saved conversation, not the current state of the filesystem. Earlier file reads come back as they were recorded. Even after compaction, Claude Code re-reads only a small number of recently used files. So with this approach the audit would reason over outdated policy text.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code sessions are saved conversations tied to a project directory. Resuming one with --continue or --resume restores the messages, tool calls, and tool results that were recorded. This is why you do not need to explain the earlier context again for a resumed task. The important point is that this restored state is a transcript, not a live view of the filesystem. A file Claude read yesterday appears in the resumed context as it was read yesterday. Nothing in the resume mechanism checks whether that file has changed on disk since then. The sessions documentation describes what is restored. The context window guide explains that even after compaction, Claude re-reads only a few recently used files. So no form of resuming guarantees fresh contents for every file Claude has read.

This gives the engineer two valid options when a teammate has changed files through git, outside Claude's own editing tools. The first option is to resume and point Claude directly at the changed files. Referencing them with an at-sign makes Claude read them before it responds. The out-of-date reads are replaced, and the rest of the understanding built up during the audit is kept. The second option is to start a fresh session and give it a structured summary of what was already found plus the names of the files that changed. This gives up the full transcript in exchange for a short, accurate starting point, and it avoids holding any outdated tool results. The right choice depends on how much of the earlier context is still valid. Resume and refresh when most of it is valid. Start fresh with a summary when the out-of-date part is large or the transcript has already been compacted several times. In both cases, the best practices recommend naming specific files and scope. Avoid asking for a broad investigation that can read hundreds of files and fill the context window.

The incorrect approaches fail in opposite directions. Assuming that claude --continue reloads every file read earlier treats the transcript as if it were kept in sync with the disk, which it is not. The audit would then reason over the old policy text and could report findings about escalation rules that no longer exist. Exploring the entire repository again in a fresh session avoids out-of-date content. But it throws away a day of valid analysis to re-check files that did not change. That is the full re-exploration this pattern is meant to avoid. Checkpoints do not help either. They track only changes made through Claude's file editing tools, not edits made by git or other external processes. The engineer has to tell Claude what changed.

QUESTION: The team wants to test a revised escalation prompt on a recorded billing-dispute session. In that session, the agent called "process_refund" against production and issued a real refund. The revised prompt may re-run turns that call tools. Which TWO actions should they plan for when they resume that session with "fork_session" enabled? (Select TWO.)
answers: Run the fork against a staging backend, since forking does not reverse a refund already processed.
Keep the original session ID on record so production can still resume it after the fork is created.
Review the production transcript afterward for the fork's new turns, since both sessions share one history.
Create the fork before the original session ends, since a finished session can no longer be branched.
feedbacks: A session is saved conversation history, not a snapshot of external state. Forking copies the transcript, including the record that process_refund was called. But it has no effect on the backend systems that already carried out that refund. So to replay write actions safely, the team must use a separate backend.

Forking creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original history and leaves the original unchanged. The fork gets its own session ID. The production record stays intact and can still be resumed separately by its original ID, so the team should keep that ID.

The two sessions share history only up to the fork point. After that, each one changes independently. Turns added in the fork are written to the fork's own transcript and are never copied back into the original. So there is nothing new to review in the production record.

Sessions are written to disk as saved transcripts. A completed session can be resumed or forked later, as long as its transcript is available on the current machine. The original session does not need to still be running.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a session is the saved conversation history: the prompt, every tool call, every tool result, and every response. It is written to disk so that an agent can get that context back later. Three options manage that history. continue picks up the most recent session in the current directory. resume targets a specific session ID. fork starts a new session that begins with a copy of the original transcript. In Python this is ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=session_id, fork_session=True). In TypeScript it is options: { resume: sessionId, forkSession: true }.

The important point is that a fork copies the history, then after that, each session changes independently. The fork gets its own session ID. Anything the replay does under the revised escalation prompt is written to the fork's transcript and nowhere else. The production session is unchanged and can still be resumed by its original ID, so the team should keep that ID on record. This is why forking is the right tool for experimenting with a real case without changing the record. But a fork is cheap only because it copies text. It does not take a snapshot of anything outside the conversation. The documentation says this clearly for the filesystem: a fork that edits files in a shared directory affects every session that uses that directory. The same logic applies to backend side effects caused through MCP tools. The original session called process_refund, so the fork inherits the record that the refund happened. But the refund itself is not reversed, and the money has already been paid. The replay may re-run turns that use tools. If the fork is connected to the production backend, it could repeat that write. So teams should connect the fork to a staging backend or make the write tools idempotent (safe to run more than once).

The other two actions misunderstand how sessions work. Forked sessions do not stay linked. After the fork, the two transcripts change independently. Turns added in the fork never appear in the original, so there is nothing to review in the production record afterward. Also, sessions are saved files, not running processes. A session that ended long ago can still be resumed or forked, if its transcript exists on the current machine or can be reached through a session store. There is no deadline tied to the end of the original session. Note also that Python has a separate fork_session() helper that can copy a transcript only up to a chosen message ID. This is useful when the replay should start right after verification instead of at the end of the recorded case. However, the fork does not carry over the original's file checkpoints.

See Agent SDK Sessions and the Python Agent SDK reference for the full fork behavior.

QUESTION: Production logs show lookup_order frequently receives a customer's email address as its identifier, and when it returns no matches the agent tells customers the order system is down. Which TWO changes most directly fix these behaviors? (Select TWO.)
answers: Add a system prompt rule reminding the agent to pass only valid order identifiers to lookup_order.
Document the accepted identifier format with an example value, such as an order number like "ORD-48213".
Explain that an empty result means no matching order exists rather than a service outage.
Configure the agent to retry lookup_order with backoff whenever it returns an empty result.
feedbacks: System prompt wording is a weaker signal than the tool's own description, and it is further away from the point of use. The model reads the tool description when it selects and calls the tool. This change also does nothing about the agent misreading empty results, so it leaves half the problem unsolved.

The description is what the model reads when it decides how to call a tool. Stating the expected input format with a concrete example directly stops the agent from passing an email where an order number belongs. This follows the documented practice of putting each parameter's meaning and format in the description itself.

A description that states this edge case tells the agent how to interpret a successful query with zero matches. The agent then stops reporting a working system as down. Documenting what the tool returns in edge cases is a core part of a complete tool description.

Retrying treats a valid empty result as if it were a temporary access failure. That is the same confusion that causes the bad behavior. A query that correctly finds nothing will find nothing again on every retry, so retries waste calls without improving the result.
prompt.explanation:
Claude chooses tools and builds their arguments almost entirely from the tool description and the input_schema. Anthropic's guidance calls the description by far the most important factor in tool performance. It recommends that the description cover what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means and what format it expects, and any limits on what the tool returns or does not return. The two failures in this scenario match two of those elements. The agent does not know what an order identifier looks like. And it does not know what a no-match result means.

Stating the input format with a concrete example, such as an order number like ORD-48213, gives the model a pattern to match before it calls the tool. An email address then no longer looks like a reasonable argument. For complex inputs or inputs with a strict format, Anthropic also offers the optional input_examples field, but the description itself is still the first thing to fix. Documenting the edge case makes clear that an empty result is a successful lookup with zero matches, not an outage. This separates a valid empty result from an access failure. With that distinction, the agent can respond correctly: it asks the customer for the right identifier instead of apologizing for a system that is working fine.

The other approaches miss how the mechanism works. A system prompt reminder is far from where the model actually reads tool guidance, and it does not address the misreading of empty results at all. Automatic retries on empty results build in the same confusion the team is trying to fix. A query that is correctly empty stays empty on every attempt. Retry logic is for temporary errors such as timeouts, not for successful queries with no matches. Read more at Define tools and Tool use overview.

QUESTION: The team split the support agent into subagents, and the one that explains statement charges received the full four-tool set. Logs show this subagent calling process_refund unprompted while describing fees. What change most directly prevents this?
answers: Have the charge-explanation subagent rate its confidence before each process_refund call and skip low-confidence ones.
Add a select_tool helper the charge-explanation subagent calls first to decide which backend tool applies.
Add a system prompt rule stating the charge-explanation subagent must never call process_refund on its own.
Remove process_refund from the charge-explanation subagent, leaving it only get_customer and lookup_order.
feedbacks: A model's rating of its own confidence is not a reliable way to judge whether an action is appropriate. A subagent that should never issue refunds has no valid high-confidence case to protect. This option adds a judgment step where no judgment should be needed.

A routing helper adds another selection step to solve a selection problem. The helper itself can still return process_refund, because the tool is still in scope. It makes the design more complex without limiting what the subagent can do.

A prompt rule relies on probabilistic compliance, meaning the model is not guaranteed to follow it. Meanwhile the tool stays available, and its description still presents refunds as a valid action. For a financial operation, leaving the capability in place and asking the model to ignore it is weaker than removing it.

Tool availability is an architectural control. A tool that is not in the subagent's set cannot be called, so the unwanted refunds become impossible, not just discouraged. Giving each subagent only the tools its role needs also makes it easier for the model to choose among the tools that remain.
prompt.explanation:
Claude does not pick tools based on an agent's job title. It picks them based on the current request and the tool descriptions it can see. A subagent whose role is to explain charges still sees process_refund, and that tool's description says it issues refunds. When a customer complains about a fee, the conversation looks a lot like a refund situation. The model has a plausible, well-described action available, and it sometimes takes it. This is the general reason why agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them. Because the tool is present, the model can take that action, and nothing about the agent's role removes that possibility.

The architectural fix is scoped tool access. Each subagent gets only the tools its role requires, plus at most a small set of utilities shared across roles. In the Agent SDK you express this in the subagent's definition, which sets its system prompt and its tool restrictions. In Claude Code, a subagent with no tools field inherits every tool available to subagents. That is how an explanation-only subagent ends up able to issue refunds. An explicit tools allowlist or a disallowedTools entry closes that gap. Removing the tool makes the wrong behavior impossible instead of unlikely, which is the right standard when the action moves money. A smaller tool set also helps the model choose among the remaining tools, because fewer tools with clear limits are less ambiguous.

The other approaches leave the capability in place. A system prompt rule asks the model to ignore a tool it can still see, whose description still invites its use. That is probabilistic compliance. It is acceptable for minor details of behavior, but not for actions with financial side effects. A confidence self-rating assumes the subagent can judge when a refund is justified. But that decision belongs to a completely different role, and model confidence is not a dependable check. A select_tool helper adds a routing step, but the helper can still name process_refund because the tool is still in scope. The problem is moved, not solved. Scoping does not replace good descriptions, however. Once the tool set is right, clear limits in each remaining tool's description still decide whether get_customer and lookup_order are chosen correctly.

See Claude Code subagents for the tools and disallowedTools fields and inheritance behavior, and Define tools for how descriptions drive selection and why fewer tools with clear limits reduce ambiguity.

QUESTION: The agent records each ticket's verified facts in a notes file. After lookup_order returns the real order total, it corrects the "refund_amount" line by calling Write with only that line, and the rest of the notes disappear. Which tool usage fixes this?
answers: Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to include the complete notes content in every Write call.
Call Edit with the stale "refund_amount" line as "old_string" and the corrected line as "new_string".
Use Bash to append the corrected line to the end of the notes file with a shell redirect.
Call Read on the notes file before Write so that Write can merge the corrected line into the existing content.
feedbacks: This relies on the model correctly reproducing the entire file on every change. That is probabilistic, meaning it is not guaranteed, and it wastes output on content that should not change. The reliable pattern is to use the tool designed for partial changes, instead of telling the model to work around a full-file tool.

Edit replaces one exact string that matches only once in the file, and it leaves the rest of the file unchanged. It is the tool built for changing one line in an existing file, which is the operation the agent needs.

Appending leaves the old refund amount in place next to the new one. The notes then contradict each other instead of being corrected. It also uses an unstructured shell operation instead of the file tools built for this task, even though Edit handles it directly.

Write always replaces the file with the full content it is given. It never appends or merges, whether or not the file was read first. Reading first meets a permission requirement for overwriting, but it does nothing to keep the existing notes.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's built-in file tools, which the Claude Agent SDK makes available to production agents, divide clearly into two kinds. Write works on the whole file, while Edit makes a targeted change. Write creates a new file, or overwrites an existing one with the full content given in the call. It does not append, and it does not merge new content with what is already on disk. In this scenario, the agent passed only the corrected refund_amount line to Write. The tool did what it is designed to do: it replaced the entire notes file with that single line.

Edit exists for partial changes to an existing file. It takes an old_string and a new_string and performs an exact string replacement. Everything else in the file stays unchanged. The matching is literal, not regex or fuzzy matching, so whitespace and indentation must match exactly. Also, old_string must occur only once in the file. If the matched text is not unique, the agent has two choices. It can add enough surrounding context to old_string to identify a single occurrence. Or it can set replace_all to true when every occurrence really should change. When a unique match is not possible, the documented fallback is to Read the full file and Write the complete changed content. This means the whole file goes through the model.

The idea that reading the file first lets Write merge content comes from a real rule that is often misunderstood. Claude must generally have read an existing file in the current conversation before Edit or Write can change it. That rule is there to prevent overwriting a file without seeing its contents. It does not change how Write behaves, and a prior read does not turn an overwrite into a merge. Telling the agent in the system prompt to always include the full file in each Write call can hide the symptom. But it depends on the model reproducing every unchanged line correctly on every call, and it spends tokens on content that should not be touched. Appending with a shell redirect through Bash leaves the outdated value in the notes. That is worse than losing it, because the agent would later read two conflicting refund amounts. In short, whole-file operations use Read and Write, targeted changes use Edit with a unique match string, and Bash is only for work the dedicated tools cannot do.

See the Claude Code tools reference for the exact behavior of Read, Write, and Edit, and the Agent SDK overview for how these built-in tools are made available to SDK-based agents.

QUESTION: The agent delegates billing dispute investigation to subagents covering order records, billing history, and refund policy. Its escalation handoffs assert conclusions like "eligible for a refund under policy" without showing which record or policy clause supports each one, so reviewers repeat every lookup. What is the structural fix?
answers: Instruct each subagent to append to the end of its summary a full list of every tool it called and every policy document it consulted.
Have the handoff step attach the most likely supporting record or policy clause to each conclusion before sending it to the reviewer.
Have each subagent return findings paired with the record or policy clause supporting each one, and keep those pairs in the handoff.
Have the agent rate its confidence in each conclusion on a numeric scale so reviewers know which ones need independent verification.
feedbacks: A list of everything consulted is a bibliography, not attribution. It does not say which record or clause supports which conclusion. Reviewers would still have to search the listed sources to work out the link, and that is the work the fix should remove.

Guessing the supporting evidence after the investigation is finished rebuilds attribution instead of keeping it. A wrong guess is worse than no reference, because it makes the conclusion look better supported than it is. Only the subagent that actually made the finding knows its true source.

Attribution is kept only when it is passed along as data. Each finding stays linked to the specific tool result or policy clause that produced it, and the coordinator merges those pairs instead of rewriting them as free-form text. The reviewer then receives conclusions that can be checked, and can confirm or override them without repeating the investigation.

Self-rated confidence is an unreliable signal, because the model can be confident and wrong. A number also gives the reviewer nothing to check against. Even perfectly calibrated scores would not tell the reviewer which record or clause the conclusion is based on.
prompt.explanation:
When a coordinator splits an investigation across subagents, each subagent works in its own isolated context. The coordinator sees only what that subagent reports back. Anthropic's own orchestration example states the result of this clearly. Subagents are told to return findings, not narration. They use a report_findings structure whose items hold claim and evidence together. This lets the orchestrator weigh and verify the findings without access to the subagent's hidden reasoning. The same principle applies to an escalation handoff. The human reviewer has no transcript, so the handoff must be self-contained. A conclusion is self-contained only when the evidence that produced it is passed along with it.

The failure in this scenario is attribution loss during compression. A subagent reads an order record and a policy clause, concludes "eligible for a refund," and then summarizes only the conclusion. Once the link is dropped, no later step can get it back. The coordinator, the handoff step, and the reviewer are all working from a statement with no source. So the structural fix is to make the finding-to-source pairing a required part of the subagent's output. For example, each item holds the finding text plus the order ID or tool result it came from, or the policy section identifier. The coordinator must then merge those pairs unchanged instead of rewriting them as free-form text. The source of each finding (its provenance) is kept from the start, never rebuilt later.

This is why the other approaches fall short. A list of every tool called and document consulted records what was read. But it does not link sources to specific conclusions, so the reviewer still has to work out the mapping again. Attaching the "most likely" supporting clause at handoff time invents attribution after the fact. In a financial dispute, a plausible but wrong citation is more dangerous than an honest gap. A confidence score adds a number the reviewer cannot audit, and a model's rating of itself is a poor signal of correctness in any case.

The Claude platform offers the same idea directly for grounding answers in documents. With Citations enabled, each response text block can carry a citations list tied to the exact passage it uses. This links each claim to its own source, instead of adding a bibliography at the end. The orchestration pattern itself is described in Build an orchestration mode. The isolation of subagent contexts, which is what makes the handoff content so important, is covered in Multiagent orchestration.

QUESTION: A customer with two open orders discusses both in one session. After mid-session compaction, the summary reads "damaged item confirmed, return eligible, $62.40 refund agreed" and the agent then calls "process_refund" against the wrong order. What change would most effectively prevent this failure?
answers: Raise the compaction threshold so the summary is generated later, after the agent has finished both refund discussions.
Require the compaction summary to keep each retained fact tied to its order ID and originating "lookup_order" result.
Have the agent rate its confidence in the order match and escalate to a human whenever the rating falls below a threshold.
Add a system prompt instruction that the agent must confirm which order a refund applies to before calling "process_refund".
feedbacks: The summary shows that the investigation was already complete. Damage was confirmed, eligibility was checked, and an amount was agreed. Changing when compaction runs does not change what the summary keeps, and a later compaction would remove the same attribution.

The summary itself shows the problem. Every fact was kept, but none of them is linked to the order record that produced it. If compaction must keep each claim linked to its source, the agent can still tell which of the two orders the refund belongs to after the earlier context is dropped.

A model's rating of its own confidence is an unreliable signal, because the agent can be confident and wrong. In this case it acted on the wrong order without hesitating. A confidence score does not restore the lost link between each fact and its order, so the ambiguity remains.

A confirmation instruction is a reasonable later safeguard, but it does not restore the information the agent needs to confirm anything. After compaction, the summary no longer says which order each fact describes. So the agent would be confirming against a guess, not a known link.
prompt.explanation:
Compaction works by replacing earlier context with a summary. From that point on, the summary is all the model has of the earlier work. Anthropic's documentation on threshold compaction says clearly that content before the compaction block is dropped on later requests. It also says that custom instructions should tell the model what the summary must keep. By default, the summary aims to keep task state (what was done and what comes next). It does not aim to keep provenance, which is the link from each finding back to the tool call, record, or statement that produced it.

That is what went wrong in this scenario. Each of the three findings in the summary is correct. But "return eligible" and "$62.40 refund agreed" no longer say which lookup_order result they describe. With two open orders, a fact without its source is ambiguous, and the agent settled the ambiguity by picking an order. This is the same mechanism that makes research reports lose citations. Compression keeps the claim and drops the claim-to-source mapping. Once the mapping is gone, it cannot be rebuilt from the summary.

So the structural fix is to make provenance part of what compaction keeps. Require every retained fact to carry its order ID and the lookup result it came from. Another way to do the same thing is to keep transaction facts, organized by order, in a persistent case-facts block that is never summarized. The other approaches do not restore the lost link. A confirmation instruction in the system prompt is a safeguard that depends on information the summary no longer contains. Raising the compaction threshold only changes when the summary is produced. The same lossy summary would be produced at any threshold. A self-rated confidence score is a poor signal, because the agent was already confident and wrong. The score also cannot restore a link that compression removed.

Anthropic's context editing guidance describes how to customize summary prompts to say what must be kept. The Agent Skills best practices show the same careful method for research: note which source supports each claim before summarizing, and check the links afterward.

QUESTION: A "PreToolUse" hook already denies "process_refund" calls above the policy cap. The team is now adding two more hooks: one that logs every refund attempt for audit, and one that approves promotional refunds. Neither new hook should be able to weaken the cap. Which TWO decisions keep the cap enforced? (Select TWO.)
answers: Keep the cap hook unchanged; a second hook returning "allow" cannot override its "deny" decision.
Move the cap check into a PostToolUse hook so it can inspect the completed refund result as well.
Implement the audit logging as an async hook, since async output cannot alter the permission decision.
State the cap in the system prompt so the promotional hook never receives an over-limit refund call.
feedbacks: When multiple PreToolUse hooks return conflicting decisions, the documented priority is deny, then defer, then ask, then allow. A promotional hook that returns allow for an over-cap refund is outranked by the existing deny. So the cap still holds without any change to the original hook.

PostToolUse runs only after the tool has run successfully, so when it fires, the refund has already been issued. It can log, add context, or change what Claude sees in the result. But it cannot prevent the original action, and preventing the action is what a cap requires.

Async hook output is meant for side effects such as logging, metrics, or notifications. Once a hook returns async output, the agent continues immediately. So an async audit hook records every attempt but can never allow, block, or change the refund call. The synchronous cap hook remains the only check that can block the refund.

A system prompt instruction is guidance that the model interprets, and compliance is probabilistic, not guaranteed. Whether an over-limit call reaches the hooks then depends on the model following the instruction. So this does not keep the cap enforced, and it is the anti-pattern that hooks exist to replace.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a PreToolUse hook is code that runs before every matching tool call and returns a permission decision before anything executes. It runs as code, not as an instruction the model reads, so its decision is deterministic. An over-cap process_refund call that the hook denies can never reach the backend. A system prompt rule is the opposite. It makes good behavior more likely, but some failures still remain. This is why Anthropic's guidance puts hard guardrails in hooks rather than in CLAUDE.md or skills.

Two less obvious properties of this mechanism decide the scenario. First, several PreToolUse hooks can fire for the same call and disagree. The SDK then settles the conflict with a fixed priority: deny outranks defer, which outranks ask, which outranks allow. So registering a promotional hook that returns allow cannot loosen the cap. The existing deny wins regardless of registration order. This layering is intentional. It means a narrower rule added later cannot quietly undo a block set at the team or application level. Second, hooks can return async output. This tells the agent to continue immediately while the hook finishes its work in the background. That makes async hooks the right design for audit logging, metrics, or notifications. It also means they are structurally unable to block or change the call, or to add context to it. If the cap decision stays synchronous and the logging is asynchronous, you get both guarantees, and neither one interferes with the other.

The remaining options fail for different reasons. PostToolUse fires after a successful execution. It is useful for converting to a standard format or shortening results before Claude sees them, but it cannot undo a refund that has already been processed. Stating the cap in the system prompt is only a request to the model. Whether an over-limit call ever reaches the hooks then depends on the model complying, not on enforcement. Note also that a hook returning allow does not skip later deny and ask rules in the permission flow, so even a permissive hook does not make the final decision. See Agent SDK Hooks for decision priority and async output, Agent SDK Permissions for the evaluation order, and Features Overview for why guardrails belong in hooks rather than instructions.

feedbacks: Starting fresh is the right pattern when earlier tool results are out of date, but in this case they are not. Re-running the lookups throws away valid, verified context. It adds latency and tool calls, and the customer has to wait while work that was already done is repeated.

The earlier context can still be trusted. The verified customer ID, the order lookup, and the return reasoning are all current, because nothing in the backend changed in twenty minutes. Resuming with the specific session ID restores that history for this customer and avoids paying for the verification steps again.

The continue option reopens the most recent session in the current directory, which is not necessarily this customer's session. prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a session is the full conversation so far: the original prompt, every tool call and result, and every response. The SDK writes it to disk automatically. So when you pick work back up, the question is whether that stored history can still be trusted. In this scenario the facts in it are still valid. Identity is verified, the order is confirmed, the backend is unchanged, and only minutes have passed. When that is true, resuming is the cheapest and most reliable path. The agent gets back its verified customer ID and order findings without spending another round of tool calls.

The SDK offers two ways to pick up earlier work. continue finds the most recent session in the current directory. This is convenient for a single developer, but it is dangerous on a shared host, where the most recent session may belong to a different customer. resume takes a specific session ID. Anthropic documents that the session_id field is present on every result message. So the application can store it for each case and reattach the correct conversation later. That is the right tool for a multi-user service.

The rule to remember is: resume when the earlier context is mostly valid; start fresh with an injected summary when earlier tool results are out of date. Results go out of date when things change outside the stored history: files are refactored, orders are updated, or policies are revised. A session saves the conversation, not the filesystem or the backend. So a long gap or a known change is the signal to start a new session and give the agent a structured summary of what was learned. Neither signal is present for this customer. Re-running lookups or pasting a raw transcript into a new session only adds cost and unneeded context. Add a sentiment classifier in front of the agent and call escalate_to_human only when the negativity score crosses a tuned threshold.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks escalate_to_human unless the customer's latest message contains the word "human" or "manager".

feedbacks: The tool description is the agent's main signal for when to call a tool, and this one tells it to escalate on any sign of displeasure. The fix is to state the real triggers: an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, or being unable to make progress. The description should also say that frustration on a routine case calls for acknowledging the feeling and then resolving the case. This fixes the cause of the behavior directly, with no new infrastructure.

Customer mood does not tell you whether a case is something the agent can handle, so a sentiment score is an unreliable signal for escalation. This option also keeps the same flawed idea that being upset should decide the handoff. It only adds a numeric threshold to it.

A keyword check breaks easily. Customers ask for a person in many different ways, and valid triggers such as policy gaps or stalled progress contain neither word, so the hook would block valid escalations. Hooks are the right tool when you need a deterministic guarantee. But this problem is a misleading description that needs correcting, not a judgment call that needs hard enforcement.

Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated. The model can be confident and wrong on hard cases, and unsure on easy ones. Adding a confidence score leaves the misleading tool description in place and replaces one unreliable signal with another.
prompt.explanation:
The agent is doing what it was told. A tool description is the main thing the model reads when it decides whether a tool fits the current situation. A description that says use when the customer seems upset turns every expression of annoyance into an escalation. Anthropic's guidance on defining tools says that the description should state not only what the tool does but also when to use it and when not to use it. The model relies on that boundary when it selects a tool. In this scenario the boundary is wrong, so rewriting it is both the cheapest change and the one that fixes the root cause.

The description should make the agent separate mood from real escalation triggers. When a customer complains about a routine return, the agent should acknowledge the frustration. Then it should deliver the concrete resolution it can provide with lookup_order and process_refund. A complaint by itself is not a reason to hand off work the agent can finish. escalate_to_human applies in three cases. The first is when the customer explicitly asks for a person. That request is honored immediately, without first trying to investigate or fix the issue. The second is when the request falls into a real policy gap. The third is when the agent cannot make progress with the tools it has. Suppose a customer who was only complaining replies to the offered resolution by saying they want a human. That is now an explicit request, and it is honored right away. Adding a few short examples of each case to the system prompt, together with the corrected description, makes the decision boundary even clearer. The customer-support guide also recommends tracking escalation accuracy along with sentiment over the conversation. Doing this lets the team confirm that the change actually raises first-contact resolution.

Each of the other approaches keeps the mistaken idea or adds machinery that does not fit the problem. A sentiment classifier still lets mood decide the handoff, only with a threshold added. But mood says nothing about whether the issue is within scope. A confidence self-rating replaces one unreliable signal with another, because the model is often confident on the very cases it gets wrong. A hook that checks for keywords looks deterministic but fails in both directions. It blocks valid escalations that do not use the exact keywords. And it still does nothing to stop the agent from choosing the tool whenever a customer sounds irritated. Programmatic checks are justified when a step must never be skipped and a miss has real consequences. When a misleading description causes poor judgment, the better fix is to correct the description.

QUESTION: This team's monorepo has a root CLAUDE.md holding TypeScript rules shared by every package. The legacy billing package alone needs extra conventions for its custom ORM. Where should those billing-only conventions be placed?

In a CLAUDE.md file inside the billing package directory, alongside the root file.
In each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so the rules follow them into the billing code.
In a copy of the root CLAUDE.md inside the billing directory, with the extra rules appended.
feedbacks: The root CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session, no matter which package is being worked on. Putting package-specific ORM rules there uses context in sessions that never touch billing code. It also makes the shared file longer, and a longer file is followed less reliably.

Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are how the hierarchy handles conventions that apply to one part of the directory tree. Claude Code loads a subdirectory CLAUDE.md on demand when it reads or edits files in that directory. Its content is added after the root file instead of replacing it. So the shared TypeScript rules still apply, and the ORM conventions are added only when work touches the billing package.

The user-level file is personal. It applies across every project on that machine and is never shared through version control. Team conventions placed there reach only the developers who add them to their own file. This is a common reason why new teammates miss instructions.

CLAUDE.md files in the hierarchy are concatenated (joined together), so the subdirectory file does not need to repeat anything from the root. Copying the shared rules puts them in context twice. It also creates two places that must be kept the same whenever the shared standards change.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's memory hierarchy has layers based on location. A user-level file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md holds personal preferences for all projects. A project-level file at the repository root (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) holds context shared by the team. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files inside subdirectories hold conventions that matter only in that part of the directory tree. These files are concatenated, not overridden. Content from the filesystem root down to the working directory is added in order. So a subdirectory file adds more specific rules on top of what the root already says. That is why the billing package file should contain only the ORM conventions and nothing from the root.

The second part of the design is lazy loading. At launch, Claude Code reads the CLAUDE.md files in the current directory and its parent directories. But CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories are loaded only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a file in that subdirectory. In a monorepo launched from the root, this means the billing conventions enter context only when billing code is being worked on. They stay out of sessions that focus on other packages. With this design, the rules are a little harder to discover, but the context stays smaller. This matters because every line in CLAUDE.md competes for the model's attention, and a shorter set of instructions is followed more reliably.

Putting the ORM rules in the root file loses that benefit and loads them into every session. Putting them in each developer's user-level file keeps them out of version control completely, so teammates who clone the repository never receive them. Copying the whole root file into the billing directory works technically. But it puts the shared rules in context twice, and the team has to maintain two copies that will become different over time. Note also that this hierarchy applies only to CLAUDE.md instruction files. .claude/settings.json is not inherited from parent directories in the same way.

See Manage Claude's memory for the hierarchy and loading rules, and Working with large codebases for monorepo guidance on per-directory CLAUDE.md files.

QUESTION: This team added "CRITICAL: You MUST run Grep before responding to ANY question" to the system prompt so the agent stops answering repository questions from memory. Now the agent runs Grep even on follow-ups like "say that more simply." What should the team change?

Set "tool_choice" to "any" so the API, rather than prompt wording, decides each turn whether Grep is invoked.
Add a PreToolUse hook that classifies each user message and blocks Grep on conversational turns.
Soften the directive to plain wording like "Use Grep when a question is about code in this repository."
feedbacks: This keeps the instruction that causes too many tool calls and tries to fix it with exceptions. The list must be extended every time a new kind of conversational turn appears. The root cause is how strong the wording is, not a missing exception, so the list treats a symptom instead of the problem.

The any mode requires Claude to call some tool on every response, so it would make the unwanted behavior worse, not better. The tool_choice parameter is the right mechanism when a tool call must be guaranteed. But in this case the goal is to let the agent answer in text when no lookup is needed.

Building a classifier and a hook to block calls that the system prompt itself demands is too much engineering for a wording problem. It also adds a second component, and its classification mistakes would now block valid code lookups.

Forceful language such as CRITICAL and MUST was used in the past to fix undertriggering, where the model did not call a tool often enough. Current guidance warns that it now causes overtriggering. The agent calls the tool on every turn because the instruction leaves no room for judgment. Plain wording that describes when the tool applies lets Claude match each request against what Grep is described to do, and answer conversational follow-ups directly.
prompt.explanation:
With the default tool_choice of auto, Claude decides on each turn whether a request matches what a tool is described to do, or whether it can answer directly. The system prompt changes how easily Claude decides to use a tool. Wording such as "Use your judgment" keeps tool use conservative. "Use the tools to investigate before responding" makes tool use more likely. Commands like "Always call a tool first" push it to the extreme. Anthropic's prompting guidance notes that aggressive phrasing ("CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...") was written to fix undertriggering on earlier models. On current models it causes overtriggering, where the tool is called when it is not needed. The documented fix is ordinary wording such as "Use this tool when...". That is what the team sees. An all-caps command that covers ANY question makes the agent run Grep on a request to rephrase an earlier answer.

System prompt wording and tool descriptions together create a probabilistic tendency, and how strong the language is matters as much as what it says. A plainly stated condition ("when a question is about code in this repository") gives the agent the behavior the team actually wants. It looks things up for repository questions and answers conversational turns from context. This is still probabilistic, so it is not guaranteed. If a specific turn truly must start with a tool call, tool_choice with any or a named tool is the mechanism that requires it. But those modes force a call. They do not prevent one. So switching to any in this scenario would guarantee a tool call on every turn, which is the opposite of the goal.

Adding an exception list keeps the forceful command in place. Maintaining the prompt then means adding more and more cases to exclude. A classifier connected to a PreToolUse hook adds infrastructure to fight the prompt's own instruction. It also creates a new way to fail, where valid code lookups are blocked because a message was classified wrongly. Fix the wording first. It is the change with the biggest effect and the lowest cost. QUESTION: This team runs Claude Code in print mode every night to list legacy modules, and a dashboard reads the output. The dashboard parser fails intermittently because the run's answer is sometimes prose or loosely formatted JSON. Which change most reliably fixes this?
answers: Add "--json-schema" with the dashboard schema to the "--output-format json" run and read "structured_output".
Wrap the run in a retry loop that re-invokes the same command until the returned output parses without errors.
Add a prompt instruction stating the answer must be valid JSON that matches the dashboard schema exactly.
Keep "--output-format json" alone and parse whatever JSON the model wrote inside the "result" text field.
feedbacks: When you supply a JSON Schema through the print-mode flag, Claude Code checks the final answer against that schema after the agent finishes its workflow. It puts the validated data in the structured_output field. Matching the schema is then a check done by the CLI, not a hope written in the prompt, and that is what a downstream parser needs.

Re-running the command until it works without changing anything treats the symptom, and it costs repeated full agent runs. Each attempt has no more constraints than the last one. The CLI already offers schema validation that produces data matching the schema, so the pipeline does not need to guess how many attempts it will take.

Prompt wording makes well-formed output more likely but cannot guarantee it, and that is the failure already seen. There is a mechanism that checks the result against a schema before it is returned. For a pipeline that runs without a person watching, relying on instructions alone is the weaker choice.

The json output format wraps the run in a JSON envelope with metadata such as the session ID. But the model's answer is in the result field as free text. Nothing about that envelope forces the text to match the dashboard schema, so the occasional parse failures would continue.
prompt.explanation:
When Claude Code runs non-interactively with claude -p, the --output-format flag controls the shape of what the CLI writes to stdout. The documented values are text (the default), json, and stream-json. Choosing json gives you an envelope that machines can read, with fields such as the session ID, usage, and cost estimates. The model's answer goes in the result field. The important point is that this envelope describes the run. It does not constrain the answer. The text inside result is whatever the model chose to write. So a dashboard parser that expects a particular object shape can still receive prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) or loosely formatted JSON.

The --json-schema flag is what turns the final answer into data that must match a schema. It is documented as print mode only. It checks the result against the supplied JSON Schema after the agent completes its workflow, and it puts the validated object in a structured_output field next to the normal metadata. This is why using --output-format json together with --json-schema is the standard pattern for CI and scheduled jobs. The pipeline reads structured_output instead of extracting data from text. Note two limits. First, the CLI refuses to start if the schema itself is not valid JSON Schema. This shows configuration mistakes early instead of at parse time. Second, the format keyword (for example "format": "email") is accepted as an annotation but not enforced. Checks of that kind still belong in your own validation code.

Reliable CI code also checks that structured_output is actually present, because a run can report success without producing structured data. It also branches on the process exit status, which is zero on success and non-zero on failure. To get the same behavior on every machine in scripted runs, Anthropic recommends --bare. With it, the job does not pick up hooks, skills, MCP servers, or CLAUDE.md files that it finds locally and that differ between machines.

Each of the other approaches has a clear weakness. Parsing the result field relies on the model's unconstrained text, which is the current failure. A stronger prompt instruction improves the chances, but it is probabilistic guidance, not validation. That is the same weakness the scenario already shows. A retry loop repeats full agent runs without adding any constraint to any attempt. It spends cost and latency on a problem that the CLI can prevent completely.

See Run Claude Code programmatically and the CLI reference for the flag details, and Agent SDK structured outputs for how schema validation and retries behave when the same agent loop is run from the SDK.
