QUESTION: This team's pipeline script runs "claude -p" to review each pull request and must parse the findings (file, line, severity, message) before posting them as inline comments. Which two practices make the output reliably machine-parseable? (Select TWO.)
answers: Instruct the prompt to reply only with valid JSON and rely on "--output-format json" by itself to enforce the findings schema.
Wrap the command in a retry loop that reruns the review until the "result" text parses as valid findings JSON.
Read the "structured_output" field from the JSON envelope instead of parsing the prose in the "result" field.
Supply the findings schema through "--json-schema" together with "--output-format json" so the run returns validated structured output.
feedbacks: The JSON output format on its own returns an envelope with fields such as "result" and "session_id". It does not check the model's answer against any schema. A prompt instruction to output JSON is probabilistic guidance, not enforcement, so the findings can still arrive malformed or with missing fields.

Re-running the whole review until the free-form text happens to parse is slow and costly. It also does not guarantee that the parsed object has the required fields. Claude Code already does schema validation and its own retries when "--json-schema" is used, and it reports a separate failure subtype if it cannot produce matching output. So a custom loop over the text field repeats weaker versions of features that already exist.

When a schema is supplied, the output that matches the schema is placed in the "structured_output" field. This is the documented contract for automation. The "result" field still holds the model's text, so parsing it would bring back the fragility that the schema was meant to remove.

The "--json-schema" flag is what makes Claude Code check the final answer against a JSON Schema after the review workflow completes. Without it, the JSON output format only wraps free-form text in an envelope. The findings then have no guaranteed shape for a script to use.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's print mode (claude -p) is how you run the agent inside scripts and pipelines. --output-format json changes the shape of what comes back. Instead of plain text, the CLI outputs a JSON envelope. It contains the model's text in result, along with metadata such as session_id. That envelope is convenient for scripting, but it says nothing about the structure of the answer itself. The output format controls the wrapper, while --json-schema controls the payload. Only when a schema is passed does Claude Code check the agent's final answer against it and put the matching object in structured_output. This is why the documented pattern pipes the response to jq '.structured_output'.

This design matters for a review pipeline because the agent still runs its normal workflow first. It can read files, grep the diff, and run tests. Only at the end must it produce JSON that matches the schema. Validation happens after the tool use completes, so you keep the full agent behavior and still get a typed result. The validation guarantees that the syntax and structure are correct, for example that required fields are present and enum values are respected. It does not guarantee that a flagged line number is correct or that a severity is well chosen. So a script that posts comments should still apply any business checks it needs. Note also that format annotations such as "format": "email" are accepted but not enforced. An invalid schema makes the CLI exit with an error before any review runs.

Reliable callers also check the outcome instead of assuming the data is always there. A result can report success without a structured_output field. If the agent cannot produce JSON that matches the schema within the retry limit, the result subtype is error_max_structured_output_retries. Treat a run as successful only when the subtype is success and structured_output exists. This keeps the comment poster from losing a run without any warning. Asking for JSON in the prompt and hoping the envelope's text parses, or looping until it does, gives up these built-in guarantees. It relies on probabilistic compliance instead and adds cost. Finally, producing findings that can be parsed is separate from the posting step. In the official GitHub Actions workflow, CLI flags are passed through claude_args, and inline comments require the GitHub comment capability to be enabled. The structured output is the input to that step. It does not replace it.

QUESTION: The team's /verify-build skill finishes by running "npm run build" and "npm run lint" on freshly generated boilerplate. Developers get a permission prompt for each command, but the team refuses to pre-approve arbitrary shell commands. What should they configure?
answers: State in the SKILL.md body that only npm scripts may be run and that no prompt is needed.
Add "allowed-tools" to the skill's frontmatter with a scoped entry such as "Bash(npm run *)".
Add "Bash" to "permissions.allow" in the project's ".claude/settings.json" so builds never prompt.
Add a bare "Bash" entry to the skill's "allowed-tools" so the commands run without prompting.
feedbacks: Claude Code itself enforces permission rules. They are not enforced by the model reading instructions, so text in the skill body cannot stop a permission prompt. The instruction may affect which commands Claude chooses, but each Bash call would still be interrupted the same way as before.

The allowed-tools field accepts the same rule format as permission rules. So an entry like Bash(npm run *) pre-approves only matching npm scripts for the turn that invokes the skill. Any other shell command still goes through the normal permission prompt. This is the balance the team asked for.

A session-wide allow rule for Bash applies to every prompt and every skill, not only to the verify-build workflow. It also covers all shell commands, not just the two npm scripts. So it applies in more places and allows more commands than the situation needs.

A bare Bash entry pre-approves every shell command Claude tries to run during the skill's turn, not just the build and lint scripts. That is the general pre-approval of any shell command that the team said it would not accept.
prompt.explanation:
A skill's allowed-tools frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) is a pre-approval list, not a sandbox. Claude Code reads it when the skill is invoked. The listed tool uses then run without a prompt for that turn. Tools that are not listed are still available, but the user's normal permission settings still apply to them. The pre-approval is also turn-scoped. It ends when the user sends the next message, even if the skill's instructions are still in the conversation. Invoking the skill again applies it again.

allowed-tools uses the same rule syntax as permission rules, so you can pre-approve a tool for specific uses instead of for everything. Entries take the form ToolName or ToolName(specifier). So Bash(npm run *) pre-approves npm scripts, while rm -rf or git push still triggers a prompt. This is why a scoped entry solves the problem in the question. The build and lint steps run without interruption, and the team's refusal to pre-approve arbitrary (unrestricted) shell commands is respected. A bare Bash entry also removes the prompts, but it allows far more. Putting Bash into permissions.allow in project settings goes further still. It applies that broad approval to every prompt and every skill in the repository.

The prompt-text approach fails for a structural reason. Claude Code's permission system is enforced by the tool harness, not by the model. Sentences in SKILL.md or CLAUDE.md can influence which commands Claude decides to run. But they cannot grant or remove tool access, so the prompts would continue. The same applies in the other direction, when you need to take tools away during a skill. allowed-tools does not do that. The disallowed-tools frontmatter field removes tools for the turn, and permissions.deny blocks them across all prompts and skills.

Two more practical notes. Workspace trust does not control a project skill's allowed-tools. So Anthropic recommends checking the pre-approvals in checked-in skills before you run Claude Code in a repository you do not know. Also, organizations can set allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly. Skill-level pre-approvals are then ignored and only managed rules apply, and /status lists any skills affected. See Claude Code Skills, Tools reference, and Permissions.

QUESTION: This team's /scaffold-module skill expects a module path and a target language, but engineers often type the command with nothing after it and receive generic output. Which SKILL.md frontmatter change best addresses this?
answers: Add "context: fork" so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and returns only its result.
Set "allowed-tools" to only the Read and Write tools so the skill cannot wander into other operations.
Add "disable-model-invocation: true" so only an engineer can trigger the skill by typing it.
Add an "argument-hint" entry so the expected arguments are shown when the command is autocompleted.
feedbacks: Running a skill in a forked context controls where its output collects. It keeps long exploration output out of the main conversation. It does nothing to tell engineers which arguments the skill needs, so running the command with no arguments would still produce generic output.

The allowed-tools field controls which tools a skill can use while it runs. It is a safety limit, not a help for entering input. Limiting tool access has no effect on whether developers supply the module path and language the skill expects.

This field stops Claude from invoking the skill on its own, while a developer can still type the slash command. It controls who can start the skill, not which arguments come with the command. So engineers would keep running it with no arguments.

The argument-hint field in the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) exists to tell developers what a skill expects, such as a module path followed by a language, at the moment they type the slash command. Showing the expected arguments during autocomplete is the documented way to reduce runs of a parameterized skill with no arguments.
prompt.explanation:
A Claude Code skill is a directory that contains a SKILL.md file. The YAML frontmatter at the top of that file configures how the skill behaves and how it is shown to users. Several frontmatter fields solve different problems. context: fork keeps long output isolated in a subagent. allowed-tools limits which tools the skill may call. disable-model-invocation keeps workflows that change things under human control. argument-hint tells users what arguments the skill expects. To choose the right field, first name the actual failure. In this scenario the failure is on the input side. Engineers do not know, or forget, that the skill needs a module path and a target language.

The documentation describes the argument-hint field as a hint shown during autocomplete to indicate the expected arguments. It is written in a form like [module-path] [language]. When an engineer starts typing /scaffold-module, the hint appears next to the command, so the engineer sees what is expected at the moment it matters. The arguments the developer then types are inserted into the skill body through placeholders such as $ARGUMENTS, $0, or $1. If the body has no placeholder, Claude Code adds an ARGUMENTS: line to the rendered content, so no arguments are lost without notice.

Be clear about the limits of this mechanism. The hint is autocomplete guidance, not validation. It does not block execution or raise an error when a developer still presses enter with nothing after the command. Numbered placeholders that have no matching argument just stay in the text as written. If a skill should not continue without its parameters, the skill's instructions can ask Claude to request the missing values before it continues. But Claude follows that kind of instruction probabilistically, so it is not guaranteed. To prevent this deterministically, you need a hook or another programmatic check, not the hint and not instructions alone. Note also that argument-hint is frontmatter specific to Claude Code. It is not accepted when you package a skill for the Skills API or for upload to claude.ai.

Each of the other fields fixes a different problem. Forking the context keeps the main conversation from filling with output. Restricting tools is about safety. Disabling model invocation controls who may start the skill. None of them tells an engineer what to type after the command. See Claude Code Skills for the full list of frontmatter fields and the argument substitution rules, and Agent Skills best practices for guidance on writing skills that are easy to invoke correctly.

QUESTION: A developer on this team wrote a /legacy-map command that summarizes an unfamiliar module's structure. It works on their machine, but teammates who pull the repository cannot invoke it; the file is at "~/.claude/commands/legacy-map.md". What should the developer do?
answers: Ask each teammate to copy the file into their own "~/.claude/commands/" directory on their machine.
Paste the command's prompt text into the project CLAUDE.md so it loads in every session.
Move the file into ".claude/commands/" in the repository and commit it with the rest of the project.
Convert the file into a skill at "~/.claude/skills/legacy-map/SKILL.md" to use the current format.
feedbacks: The home directory location is personal configuration that is never shared through version control, so this works only until the next change. Each change to the command would have to be copied again by hand, and the team's copies would soon become different from each other.

CLAUDE.md supplies project context that is always loaded. It does not define a slash command that can be invoked. Teammates would still have no /legacy-map to run. Also, a workflow that is needed only sometimes would now take up context in every session, whether or not it is needed.

The scope of a command depends on where the file is stored. A markdown file in the repository's .claude/commands/ directory is project-scoped and is shared through version control. It becomes /legacy-map for every teammate as soon as they pull.

Changing from the legacy command format to a skill does not change the scope. A skill in the home directory is still personal configuration that git never sees. So the developer would still be the only person able to run /legacy-map.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code decides the scope of a custom slash command only from the location of its file. A markdown file in .claude/commands/ inside the repository is project-scoped. It is committed together with the code, and every developer who clones or pulls the repository gets the command automatically. The file name (without .md) becomes the command name. A file in ~/.claude/commands/ is user-scoped. It is available to one person in all of their projects and is never seen by git. In this question, the command works for its author and for nobody else. That is the typical sign of a project workflow that was created in the personal location.

The .claude/ directory in a repository is where the team keeps its shared configuration, while ~/.claude is a private layer on top of it. Anything that should be part of how the team works together belongs in the repository. This includes shared commands, the project CLAUDE.md, project rules, and skills. These are reviewed and versioned like any other code. Anything that reflects one person's habits belongs in the home directory. Having both layers is deliberate. Individuals can keep personal tools without forcing them on colleagues. And the team can improve shared tools through normal pull requests instead of sending each other files.

That last point is why copying the file by hand into each teammate's home directory does not solve the problem. It gives a working command for a short time, but there is no longer one source of truth. Every improvement must be sent out again by hand, and the copies will become different over time. Pasting the prompt into the project CLAUDE.md does share it through version control. But CLAUDE.md is guidance that is always loaded, not a command definition. Nobody gets a /legacy-map to invoke, and a workflow used only sometimes now uses context in every session. Converting the file into a skill in ~/.claude/skills/ changes the format but not the scope. The home directory is personal whether it holds a command file or a skill directory, so the result is the same problem the team already has.

Note that the .claude/commands/ format is the legacy form and is still fully supported. But current Anthropic guidance recommends Agent Skills at .claude/skills/NAME/SKILL.md for new work, because a skill directory can include supporting files and options set in the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file). Both forms create a /NAME command, and both follow the same scope rule: in the repository for the team, in the home directory for one person. See The .claude directory reference and Skills in Claude Code.

QUESTION: A developer gave the agent three sample rows with expected outputs to fix null handling in a migration script. The returned fix checks for those exact three values with explicit conditionals. What should the developer do next?
answers: Ask for a general solution that handles all valid inputs, treating the sample rows as verification only.
Repeat the request with stronger wording insisting that the fix must handle nulls correctly in all cases.
Have the agent rate its confidence that the fix generalizes and retry the request whenever the rating is low.
Supply additional sample rows until every value the production data could contain is represented in the examples.
feedbacks: Claude can focus too much on making the given cases pass and hardcode their specific values. The explicit conditionals show this happened. The documented fix is to state that the examples are for verification and are not the specification. Then ask for a general-purpose solution that works for every valid input, and confirm that it still passes the samples.

The fix already handles nulls correctly for the cases it was shown, so stressing correctness does not address the real problem. The agent needs to be told that the examples show a general rule and are not the complete set of inputs.

Self-reported confidence is unreliable because a model can be confident and wrong. A fix that passes every example it has seen will probably rate itself highly. Retrying without changing the instruction tends to repeat the same behavior of matching the examples.

More rows do not change how the agent understands the task. It can keep adding one conditional for each example. Production data cannot all be listed in advance, so a fix that covers only listed values will still fail on the first row it has not seen.
prompt.explanation:
Concrete input and output examples are the most effective way to explain an edge-case requirement. But they have a known failure mode. The model may treat the examples as the entire problem and write code that recognizes those specific inputs, instead of the rule they show. Explicit conditionals that check for the three sample values are the typical sign of this overfitting to examples. Anthropic's prompting guidance names this problem directly. It recommends asking for a general-purpose solution that works for all valid inputs, and making clear that the tests exist to verify the solution, not to define it.

The examples and tests have one role, and the written request has another. Examples and tests are verification. The written request is the specification. When the developer says "these three rows must produce these outputs," the agent has only the verification part. It fills in the specification by matching what it sees. The developer can fix this with one sentence that describes the samples as typical cases of a general null-handling rule. The developer should also ask the agent to run the samples as tests after it implements that rule. This puts each part back in its intended role. The same guidance also advises telling Claude not to remove or edit tests, because weakening a check is another way a fix can appear to pass.

The other approaches miss the cause. Adding more and more sample rows keeps the agent focused on listing cases one by one, and it still cannot cover data that has not been seen yet. Stronger wording about correctness repeats a goal that the agent believes it has already met for every case it was given. Self-rated confidence is a weak signal that will be high for this kind of fix. Retrying with the same prompt tends to produce the same behavior. See Claude prompting best practices for the guidance on avoiding hardcoded test-passing, and Claude Code common workflows for the recommended cycle: write tests for specific behavior, implement, and then run the tests to confirm.

QUESTION: A team stores its legacy-module conventions in a ".claude/rules/" file with "paths: [\"src/legacy/**/*\"]". In a fresh session, before any file is opened, Claude cannot describe those conventions when asked. The team wants them available from launch in every session. What should they change?
answers: Move the rule into a ".claude/rules/legacy/" subdirectory so discovery picks it up at launch.
Add explicit file extensions to the glob, since a bare directory pattern matches nothing.
Have engineers run /memory at the start of each session to register the rule file.
Remove the "paths" field from that rule so it loads at launch like an unscoped rule.
feedbacks: Claude Code already finds Markdown files under .claude/rules/ recursively, so the file is found wherever it is in that directory tree. Its location does not change what makes it load. As long as the rule keeps its paths field, it still waits until a matching file is read or edited.

Directory globs such as src/**/* are a documented pattern form for the paths field, and they match every file below that directory. Extensions are optional. They are needed only when a rule should apply to a specific file type. So this change would not affect when the rule loads.

The /memory command is a tool for checking and editing memory files. It does not register or activate rules. Unscoped rules load at launch, and path-scoped rules load when a matching file is accessed. No manual registration step is involved.

A rule with a paths field is not put into context at launch. It is loaded when Claude uses Read, Write, or Edit on a file that matches the glob. Removing the paths field makes the rule load at session start in all cases, which is what the team wants. The cost is that those conventions are then in the context of every session.
prompt.explanation:
In .claude/rules/, each Markdown file is a block of instructions with its own loading trigger. A rule file with no frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) acts like part of CLAUDE.md. It is read at launch and stays in context for the whole session. Adding a paths field in YAML frontmatter changes that trigger. The rule is not loaded until Claude actually works with a matching file. That can happen through Read, Write, or Edit, or by viewing a single matching file with a Bash command that reads files, such as cat. Until then, the conventions are not in the model's context at all. So when the team asks a question before any legacy file is opened, Claude cannot report them.

The feature is designed around this tradeoff. Loading every convention into every session costs tokens. It also spreads the model's attention across rules that do not apply to the current work. Scoping rules by path keeps the context small and lets Claude focus on the rules that matter for the files it is working on. The cost is what the team saw: scoped rules are lazy, meaning they load only when needed. So general questions asked at the start of a new session will not reflect them. When a convention should be available at all times, leave the paths field off that rule (or put the content in the project CLAUDE.md) and accept the cost of having it in context all the time. Do not expect a scoped rule to be present before a matching file is used.

Each of the other changes misunderstands what activates the rule. Directory globs like src/**/* are a documented pattern form and match all files below the directory. So adding extensions does not change when the rule loads. /memory is a way to view and edit memory files, not a switch that registers rules. And rule discovery under .claude/rules/ is already recursive. If the file is moved into a subdirectory, it is found in the same way and keeps the paths trigger. See Manage Claude's memory for how path-scoped rules load and The .claude directory for where rule files are stored.

QUESTION: The agent is automating a dependency upgrade across 40 services and cannot resolve one legacy module without a decision from its owning engineer, who cannot see the agent's session. What should the handoff to that engineer contain?
answers: A structured summary naming the module, the root cause found so far, the failing error, and a recommended fix.
The complete raw outputs of every Grep, Read, and Bash call the agent ran, so no evidence is left out.
An urgency score and the agent's self-rated confidence in its own analysis, so the engineer can prioritize the case.
Only the module name and a short issue label, so the engineer investigates without the agent's bias.
feedbacks: The receiving engineer has no access to the session, so the handoff must be self-contained. It names the exact module, states what the agent found about the cause, includes the concrete failing error, and proposes a next step. This passes on the full state of the case, so the engineer can decide quickly instead of repeating the investigation.

Raw tool output passes on unprocessed noise. It moves the analysis work to the engineer, who must work out again what the agent already concluded. Forwarding everything also becomes worse as sessions grow, because most of that content is not relevant to the decision being requested.

Urgency and confidence ratings describe the agent's view of the case, not what the case is. A model's self-rated confidence is also an unreliable signal. Without the module, root cause, error, and recommendation, the engineer still cannot act on the escalation.

Holding back the completed investigation forces the engineer to find the root cause and the failing error again from the start. This wastes the work the agent already did. The purpose of a handoff is to pass on findings, not to hide them so that the engineer can form an independent view.
prompt.explanation:
Escalation in an agentic system is a problem of state transfer, meaning passing the current state of the work to someone else. The agent has used many tool calls to build up an understanding of the situation. But that understanding exists only in its own conversation history. The Messages API is stateless. Every turn carries the full history that your application chooses to send, and nothing is stored on Claude's side for a person to look up later (see Working with messages). When the receiving engineer cannot see that session, the only context they will ever have is what the agent writes into the handoff.

That is why the documented pattern is a structured handoff summary. It is a self-contained document with these parts: the identifiers (in this case the module and service, not a customer ID), the root cause analysis so far, the concrete values that matter (the exact failing command or error, not a refund amount), and a recommended action. The same structure applies whether the agent is handing a billing dispute to a support lead or a stuck migration to a module owner. The goal is that the person can decide and act without running the investigation again. This keeps escalation cheap enough to use whenever it is needed.

Forwarding raw Grep, Read, and Bash output is a tempting alternative because it seems fully transparent. But it gives the engineer a large amount of evidence and none of the conclusions, so a person has to redo the analysis. The output also keeps growing with no limit. Anthropic's context-window guidance notes that accuracy and recall degrade as the number of tokens rises, and a human reader has the same problem with too much text (Context windows). Sending only a module name and label throws away the completed work completely. Urgency and self-rated confidence scores describe the agent's attitude toward the case, not the case itself. A model's confidence in itself is also not a dependable measure of how hard a problem really is.

In practice, teams make the handoff reliable by requiring it in a fixed JSON shape. Structured Outputs with output_config.format and a JSON schema let you require fields such as module_path, root_cause, failing_error, and recommended_action. The escalation queue then always receives complete records that can be parsed. Keep sensitive values in the message content, not in the schema definition itself (Structured outputs).

QUESTION: The billing maintainers added "@standards/billing.md" to "packages/billing/CLAUDE.md" to pull in a shared file from the root-level standards/ directory, but /memory shows the standards file never loads. How should they fix the import while keeping it scoped to their package?
answers: Start every Claude Code session from the repository root so the import resolves against that directory.
Move the import into the repository root CLAUDE.md, where "@standards/billing.md" resolves correctly.
Rewrite the path relative to the package CLAUDE.md, such as "@../../standards/billing.md".
Wrap the path in double quotes so Claude Code reads the whole path as a single import token.
feedbacks: Relative import paths are not resolved from the working directory. So launching from the root does not change where "@standards/billing.md" points. The path is still resolved from packages/billing/ and still does not find the file.

The path would resolve correctly from the root. But the root CLAUDE.md is loaded for every session anywhere in the monorepo. That puts billing-specific standards into every package's context. It also loses the per-package selection that the maintainers want to keep.

Relative import paths are resolved from the directory of the file that contains the import, not from the process working directory. The file is in packages/billing/, so the path must go up two levels to reach the root standards/ directory (or use an absolute path). The import then stays limited to the billing package's own CLAUDE.md.

Putting quotes around an import path does not make it import. The documented way to handle spaces in a path is to escape them with a backslash, and this path has no spaces anyway. The failure is about how the path is resolved, not about how it is split into tokens, so quotes do not help.
prompt.explanation:
The @path import syntax lets a package's CLAUDE.md pull in only the shared standards that its maintainers know apply to their code. The imported files are expanded into context at launch, together with the file that references them. The detail that confuses people is where a relative path starts from. It is resolved relative to the file that contains the import, not relative to the directory where Claude Code was started. So a CLAUDE.md in packages/billing/ that says @standards/billing.md is looking for packages/billing/standards/billing.md. That file does not exist, so nothing loads. Rewriting it as @../../standards/billing.md, or using an absolute path, points to the real file. The import also stays inside the billing package's own instruction file.

This resolution rule is deliberate. A per-package CLAUDE.md is meant to be self-describing and portable. Its imports should mean the same thing whether a session was launched from the repository root or from inside the package. Package owners should be able to understand their file without knowing how colleagues launch their sessions. If paths were resolved from the working directory, the same file would behave differently from one session to the next.

Each of the other approaches fails. Moving the import to the root CLAUDE.md does make the path resolve. But the root file is loaded for every session in the repository, so billing rules would be in every package's context. The purpose of selective per-package imports would be lost. Launching from the repository root changes nothing, because relative imports are not resolved from the working directory. Quoting the path misreads the syntax rules. Quoted paths are not imported at all, and backslash escaping is only for paths that contain spaces.

Keep two more limits in mind. Imports organize instructions, but they do not reduce context cost, because everything imported still loads at launch. So files that matter only for part of a codebase are often better placed in path-scoped .claude/rules/ files. Also, recursive imports are supported only to a limited depth, so standards files that import each other through many levels should be combined into fewer levels. See Manage Claude's memory and Working with large codebases for the full import and monorepo guidance.

QUESTION: The MCP code-index server used by this system returns an empty list from "find_references" both when a symbol has no callers and when the index is mid-rebuild. As a result, the agent retries when a symbol truly has no callers, and when the index is rebuilding, it wrongly decides the symbol is unused. Which tool change fixes this?
answers: Return a successful empty list for no matches, and an error marked transient and retryable when the index is unavailable.
Keep returning an empty list in both cases but record the index state in server logs so the team can audit mistaken conclusions.
Instruct the agent in its system prompt to retry any empty result three times before treating the symbol as unreferenced.
Return an error flagged retryable for both cases so the agent always retries once more before concluding the symbol is unused.
feedbacks: A symbol with no callers is a valid, complete answer, so it should come back as a normal successful result. An unavailable index is an access failure. It should be flagged with "isError" and marked as a transient (temporary), retryable condition. When the tool returns these two cases differently, the agent gets a clear signal. It stops retrying real answers, and it stops treating an empty result during a rebuild as evidence.

Server-side logging helps the team see what happened afterward, but it gives the agent nothing at the moment it decides. So the retries and the false conclusions continue unchanged. Returning a successful empty result when the backend was actually unavailable hides the error without any signal, and this turns a failure into wrong information.

A prompt rule cannot tell the two cases apart, because the tool response itself contains no information that separates them. The agent would use three calls on every symbol that truly has no callers. It could also still be misled if a rebuild lasts longer than the three retries.

Marking a real empty result as an error labels a correct answer as a failure. This guarantees wasted retries on every symbol with no references. It also still does not tell the agent whether the index was actually available. An empty result during a rebuild, followed by another empty result during a rebuild, would again be taken as proof.
prompt.explanation:
The problem in this scenario is that one response shape has two very different meanings. One meaning is the query succeeded and found nothing. The other is the query could not be answered right now. An agent can make a correct retry decision only when it can tell these two outcomes apart, because the right reaction to each is the opposite of the other. A valid empty result is final and should be accepted. An access failure, such as an index rebuild or a timeout, is transient (temporary) and should be retried or handled later.

MCP gives tools a separate channel for this distinction. A tool execution error is a normal JSON-RPC result whose isError field is true. The specification describes these results as feedback the model can act on to correct itself, as documented in the MCP Tools specification. The fields the protocol defines are content, structuredContent, and isError. Retry policy metadata, such as an error category or a retryable flag, is not a built-in protocol field. An application defines it in its own structured result or output schema. So the design pattern has two parts. When the symbol really has no references, return a plain successful result (an empty array). When the index is unavailable, return an error result whose content says that the index is unavailable, that the condition is transient, and that retrying later is appropriate. The same idea applies on the client side when results are passed back to Claude. The tool result handling guidance shows that failures are sent as a tool_result with is_error set, and Claude adjusts its next action to the specific error text it receives.

The other approaches all fail because they work at the wrong layer or in the wrong direction. Flagging both cases as retryable errors turns every symbol with no references into a guaranteed wasted retry. It also still leaves the rebuild case impossible to detect. A prompt instruction to retry empty results three times cannot see information the tool never sends. It adds a fixed cost to every real empty result and gives no guarantee during a long rebuild. Logging the index state on the server is useful for audits. But from the agent's point of view, it hides the error without any signal, because the agent still receives a success that it should not trust. QUESTION: The coordinator in this system delegates legacy-codebase exploration with a prompt that lists exact steps: glob src for every file, grep each import, then read files in order. On repositories with unusual layouts, subagents follow the script literally and miss the real architecture. How should the coordinator prompt be revised?
answers: Have the coordinator rerun the same instructions whenever a subagent's summary comes back incomplete.
Add numbered steps covering each new repository layout so the procedure handles every structure encountered so far.
Describe the exploration goal and quality criteria, letting each subagent choose its own investigation path.
Raise each subagent's turn and context budget so it can finish the scripted procedure on larger repositories.
feedbacks: Repeating the same delegation produces the same scripted behavior and the same gaps, at double the token cost. Retries help with transient (temporary) failures. They do not help with a prompt that always directs the subagent to the wrong exploration strategy.

Adding more layouts to the script keeps the prompt procedural, and it covers only structures already seen. So the next unfamiliar repository fails in the same way. Step-by-step lists are appropriate when the order or completeness of the steps really matters. They are not appropriate for open-ended investigation, where the right steps depend on what is found.

A goal-oriented prompt tells the subagent what a good result looks like without saying how to get there. For example, it can ask the subagent to identify entry points, trace the main dependency flow, and cite a file path for every claim. The subagent can then adapt how it uses Glob, Grep, and Read to whatever layout it finds. This is the flexibility the scripted procedure lacks.

A bigger budget lets the subagent carry out more of a procedure that is wrong for the repository. It reads more irrelevant files instead of finding the architecture. The failure is in the instructions, not in resource limits, and more capacity does not change what the subagent is told to do.
prompt.explanation:
The main design choice in a coordinator prompt is whether to tell subagents what to achieve or how to do it. Anthropic's prompting guidance recommends being clear and specific about the desired output and constraints. But it recommends numbered procedural steps only when the order or completeness of the steps really matters. It also clearly advises using general instructions instead of step-by-step instructions for work that needs a lot of reasoning. Codebase exploration is open-ended. The useful sequence of Glob, Grep, and Read calls depends on whether the repository is a monorepo, a single package, a generated-code project, or something more unusual. A fixed script follows the investigation path for one layout and fails on every other layout.

A prompt that states the goal and the criteria works because it gives the subagent a target to reason toward and a standard to check itself against. For example, the prompt can state that the result must identify entry points, trace the main dependency flow, and cite a concrete file path for each claim. The model can then choose its own approach and still produce output that the coordinator can validate. This also fits how Agent SDK subagents work. Each one runs in a fresh, isolated context and returns only its final report. So the delegation prompt should contain the goal, any known limits, and the quality standard, not a fixed recipe that breaks easily.

The other options keep the procedural structure. Adding more numbered steps for each layout covers only repositories already seen. Raising the subagent's turn or context budget lets it follow the wrong plan for longer, and it uses tokens on files that do not answer the question. Rerunning the same instructions when the summary is incomplete only repeats the same scripted behavior. Retries address transient failures, not a prompt that always sends the subagent in the wrong direction.

See Claude prompting best practices for guidance on general versus step-by-step instructions and on success criteria for research, and Subagents in the SDK for how delegation prompts and isolated subagent context work.

QUESTION: A team adds ".claude/rules/terraform.md" whose YAML frontmatter sets "paths: ["terraform/**/*"]". In a fresh session, before any file is opened, Claude does not apply the Terraform conventions when asked about them. The team wants these conventions available from the first message. What should they do?
answers: Change the glob to "../../terraform/**/*" so it resolves relative to the rule file's location.
Add a line to the rule marking the conventions as IMPORTANT so Claude prioritizes them.
Rewrite the "paths" value as a comma-separated string instead of a YAML list so it parses.
Remove the "paths" frontmatter from the rule so it loads unconditionally at session start.
feedbacks: Glob patterns in project rules are resolved relative to the directory that contains the .claude folder, not relative to the rule file's own location. The pattern terraform/**/* is correct as written. A ../../ prefix would point outside the repository, and the rule would still be path-scoped.

Emphasis only raises the priority of text that is already in context. The path-scoped rule is not loaded at all until a matching file is read or edited. So stronger wording inside it has no effect on the first message.

Claude Code accepts paths either as a YAML list or as a comma-separated string, so the list form in the rule is valid and already parses. Changing the syntax keeps the rule path-scoped. It would still wait for activity on a matching file before loading.

A rule with a paths field is not added to context when the session starts. It is loaded on demand when Claude uses Read, Write, or Edit on a file that matches the pattern. Removing the paths field from the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) makes the rule unscoped. Its conventions then load at launch, like the project-root CLAUDE.md, and are present before any Terraform file is used.
prompt.explanation:
There are two kinds of files in .claude/rules/. A rule with no paths frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) is unscoped. It always loads when the session starts, in the same way as the project-root CLAUDE.md. A rule whose frontmatter declares paths is path-scoped. Claude Code removes the frontmatter and waits to load the body until Claude actually works with a matching file. That happens through the Read, Write, or Edit tool, or when Claude views a single matching file with a Bash command such as cat or head. The design goal is to save context. Conventions for Terraform, tests, or a particular service use no tokens in sessions that never touch those files.

That tradeoff explains the behavior in this scenario. The developer asked a general question before any Terraform file was read or edited, so nothing had triggered the rule yet. As soon as Claude opens a file under terraform/, the conventions are loaded. The team wants those conventions present from the first message, whatever files are used. So the fix is to remove the paths field, which makes the rule unscoped. Moving the content into the project-root CLAUDE.md gives the same always-loaded result. The same on-demand loading applies after /compact. Unscoped rules and CLAUDE.md are added again from disk, while path-scoped rules load again only when their trigger file is used again.

Each of the other approaches misunderstands how rules are parsed, resolved, or applied. The paths field accepts both a YAML list and a comma-separated string. So rewriting the syntax changes nothing, and the rule stays path-scoped. Globs in project rules are interpreted relative to the directory that contains the .claude folder. So terraform/**/* is already correct, and a ../../ prefix would point outside the repository. Adding emphasis such as IMPORTANT only changes the priority of instructions that are already in context. A rule that has not loaded cannot be given priority. One more limit to remember: if the YAML between the frontmatter markers fails to parse, Claude Code treats the rule as unscoped without any warning. This causes the opposite symptom, where the rule loads everywhere. claude --debug shows the parse error.

See Manage Claude's memory for path-specific rule syntax and loading triggers, and Context window for how scoped rules behave across compaction.

QUESTION: An engineer asks the agent to map every cross-module dependency in a legacy monolith before a refactor. Grep and Read results flood the main conversation, and the context is nearly exhausted before the design discussion even begins. How should the discovery phase be run?
answers: Run /compact repeatedly during the discovery phase so the accumulated search output gets summarized as it grows.
Delegate the discovery phase to the Explore subagent and bring only its summary into the main conversation.
Move the investigation into plan mode so the read-only exploration generates less output.
Start a fresh session for each module and carry the findings forward by hand between sessions.
feedbacks: Compaction summarizes the history after the long output is already in the main conversation. Each summary can also drop exact file paths, counts, and other precise details that a dependency map needs. It treats the symptom instead of keeping the discovery output out of the main context from the start.

The Explore subagent is a read-only agent built for codebase search and analysis, and it runs in its own context window. The hundreds of search results and file contents stay inside that isolated context. Only a short summary returns to the main conversation. This leaves room for the design and implementation work that comes next.

Plan mode prevents edits while Claude researches. But it does not change how much tool output the research produces or where that output collects. Every Grep and Read result still goes into the main conversation, so the context fills up just as quickly.

Splitting the investigation across sessions keeps each context smaller. But it breaks the picture of cross-module dependencies into separate parts, and it relies on copying by hand, which loses detail and continuity. A subagent gives the same isolation without breaking the shared context that the later design phase needs.
prompt.explanation:
The main purpose of Claude Code subagents is context isolation, not only task specialization. A subagent runs in its own context window. Some side tasks would fill the main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents. If you delegate such a task, those raw results stay in the subagent's context, and only a summary or result comes back. The built-in Explore subagent is designed for this pattern. It is a fast, read-only agent optimized for finding files, searching code, and exploring a codebase. Its tools are read-only, and Write and Edit are denied. So it can map a legacy monolith's dependencies without ever changing it. When Claude invokes it, Claude sets a thoroughness level (quick, medium, or very thorough). To keep research fast and cheap, Explore also starts without the user, project, or local CLAUDE.md files, and without the git status snapshot.

For a task with several phases, use main-conversation context for the phases where shared context is most valuable. For example, design the refactor together with the engineer and then implement it consistently. Move long, self-contained discovery work into a subagent. The isolation has costs. The returned summary still enters the main conversation. Each subagent uses tokens while it runs, and those requests count toward the same usage limits. So many subagents that return detailed results can still use a lot of space. A built-in Explore run cannot be continued later. Explore returns no agent ID and cannot be resumed. If you need to continue the work later, a general-purpose or custom subagent is a better choice.

The other approaches miss how the mechanism works. Running /compact repeatedly summarizes history only after the long output has already used up the main context. Summarization can also drop exact numbers, paths, and dates without any warning, and a dependency map relies on them. Plan mode makes exploration read-only. It is useful for defining the scope of a large refactor before making changes. But it does nothing to keep tool output out of the main conversation. Splitting the work into separate sessions and copying findings by hand keeps each context small. But it breaks the cross-module picture into pieces and loses continuity between discovery and design. See Claude Code subagents and Context window for how subagents keep large reads out of the main context.

QUESTION: A developer on this team has fallen into the habit of starting every Claude Code task in plan mode. The next task is renaming a misspelled helper function that is defined and called within a single file. How should the developer handle this task?
answers: Fork the session into two branches so alternative names can be compared before committing.
Delegate the rename to an Explore subagent so its search output stays out of the main context.
Enter plan mode so Claude maps every reference before proposing the rename for approval.
Execute the rename directly, since the change is fully scoped and needs no exploration first.
feedbacks: Forking a session is useful when two really different approaches start from the same investigation and need to be explored separately. Correcting a misspelling has one obvious result. Running parallel branches adds extra steps to a task that has no competing designs to compare.

The Explore subagent keeps long discovery output out of the main conversation during multi-phase tasks, so the main context window does not fill up. Finding one function in one file produces almost no output. There is nothing to keep out of the main context, and the extra delegation step only slows the task down.

Plan mode is the right tool when the approach is uncertain, when many files are affected, or when the code is unfamiliar. None of these applies to a rename inside one file. Forcing a read-only exploration phase and an approval step for this task adds a review cycle but does not reduce any real risk.

A rename inside one file is a change whose diff can be described in a single sentence. There is no uncertainty about the approach and no unfamiliar code to understand. Plan mode exists so that Claude can analyze before committing to large or unclear changes. The official guidance names renaming a variable as a case where planning only adds overhead.
prompt.explanation:
Plan mode in Claude Code is a permission mode. It is not a habit to apply to every task. While plan mode is active, Claude reads files, runs exploratory commands, and writes a proposed plan. It does not edit source files until the user approves that plan. This restriction is the purpose of plan mode: it adds safety and review for changes where a mistake is expensive. Examples are architectural restructuring, migrations that touch dozens of files, tasks with several possible approaches, and work in code the developer does not yet understand.

This safety has a cost: an extra round trip. Every plan-mode task needs a read-only exploration phase, a plan for the user to read, and an approval step before any edit is made. For a rename inside a single file, this overhead gives no benefit. There is no design decision to get wrong and no unfamiliar code to explore. Anthropic's guidance states the boundary clearly: if you can describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Typo fixes, added log lines, and variable renames are the standard examples where direct execution is preferred. Whether to use plan mode depends on how uncertain the approach is, how many files change, and how unfamiliar the code is. It does not depend on how careful a developer wants to feel.

Each of the other approaches uses a tool that was built for a different problem. The Explore subagent protects the main context window from long discovery output in multi-phase work, and a lookup in one file produces almost none. Forking a session lets two approaches develop separately from a shared investigation, which only makes sense when there is a real choice between approaches. Entering plan mode for the rename is the most tempting mistake, because planning rarely causes harm. But it turns a ten-second edit into a propose-and-approve cycle without lowering any risk. If you save plan mode for the tasks that match its documented triggers, the review step stays meaningful for the tasks where it is needed.

See Claude Code Best Practices for the explore, plan, implement workflow and when to skip planning, and Permission Modes for how plan mode blocks edits until approval.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: In about 8% of runs the coordinator spawns the report-generation subagent before the synthesis subagent has returned its cited findings, despite a system prompt instruction requiring synthesis first, so those reports ship without citations. What change guarantees the required ordering?
answers: Have the report-generation subagent rate its confidence that citations are complete before returning.
Add few-shot examples to the coordinator prompt showing synthesis completing before report generation.
Add a "PreToolUse" hook that rejects "Task" calls to the report generator until synthesis output exists.
Rewrite the ordering instruction in bold at the top of the coordinator's system prompt.
feedbacks: A self-rated confidence score does not change when the report generator is spawned. If synthesis never ran, the subagent has no citations to assess. A model's rating of its own work is not a reliable measure of correctness, and it does nothing to control the order of the workflow.

Few-shot examples are a real technique for making behavior more consistent, and they would probably reduce the failure rate. But they are still guidance that the model follows most of the time. They do not block the out-of-order call, so reports without citations can still ship.

A PreToolUse hook runs in code before the tool call executes, and it can deny the call. While the synthesis output is missing, the hook blocks the Task tool call that would spawn the report generator. The ordering rule changes from something the coordinator usually follows into something it cannot skip. That is what the scenario requires.

Emphasis and placement make an instruction more important compared to other instructions. But the model still follows it probabilistically, which means compliance is not guaranteed. The scenario already shows the coordinator ignoring a prompt instruction in a measurable share of runs. Stronger wording lowers that rate, but it cannot guarantee that the rate reaches zero.
prompt.explanation:
This scenario is a workflow ordering problem with a strict requirement: the report generator must not run until synthesis has produced cited findings. The coordinator already has a prompt instruction that says this, and the logs show that it ignores the instruction in a measurable fraction of runs. This data point is the most important signal. Anything in the system prompt (restated, in bold, or shown with examples) is guidance that the model follows with high, but not perfect, reliability. Anthropic's guidance on CLAUDE.md and memory makes the same distinction. Those files are treated as context, not as enforced configuration. When an action must be blocked no matter what Claude decides, the documented tool is a PreToolUse hook.

In the Claude Agent SDK, hooks are callback functions that you pass in the agent options. A PreToolUse callback runs before the tool call executes and returns a decision. If several hooks return different decisions, deny wins over defer, ask, and allow. Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, and the coordinator's allowed tools must include it before it can delegate at all. So the coordinator's attempt to launch the report generator is itself a tool call that the hook can inspect. The hook checks whether synthesis output exists and denies the call if it does not. The coordinator receives the denial as feedback and changes the order of its work, and the blocked call never executes. The guarantee is narrow but real. The hook does not make the coordinator plan better. It only makes the out-of-order action impossible.

Use hooks for rules that must never be broken, and use prompts for preferences and nuance. Prompt emphasis and few-shot examples are good tools when flexibility matters or when an occasional miss costs little. In this scenario, a miss produces a shipped report with no citations, which defeats the purpose of the system. Asking the report generator to rate its own confidence does not address the cause or the timing. The subagent is already running too early, and a model's rating of itself cannot reliably replace a check that blocks the call. Note also that a PostToolUse hook is the wrong event for this rule. It fires after the tool has already run, so it cannot prevent the spawn.

See Claude Agent SDK hooks, Claude Code hooks reference, and CLAUDE.md and memory for the distinction between guidance and enforcement.

answers: Add a system prompt instruction telling the coordinator to avoid spawning subagents it does not need.
Rewrite the subagent's description to state it applies only when source documents are supplied.
Restrict the document analysis subagent's tools to Read and Grep so unnecessary runs cost less.
Hard-code the pipeline so the document analysis subagent always runs after web search completes.
feedbacks: The coordinator is already trying to delegate only when needed. The problem is that the description does not tell it when document analysis is relevant. A general instruction to be more selective does not add this missing information about when the subagent applies, so the coordinator keeps delegating too often.

The coordinator reads a subagent's description to decide whether to invoke it. A vague description that could match any request causes the subagent to be spawned for almost everything. If the description names the condition that actually calls for this subagent (supplied source documents), the coordinator has the information it needs to skip it on web-only questions.

Tool restrictions limit what a subagent can do once it is running. They have no effect on whether the coordinator chooses to spawn it. The subagent would still be invoked on web-only requests and would still use its own API calls and context.

A fixed pipeline removes the coordinator's ability to analyze each request and choose only the subagents it needs. This is the opposite of dynamic selection. It also still runs document analysis on every request, so the wasted work that the logs showed does not go away.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent is defined with an AgentDefinition. Its description is not decoration. It is the main signal the parent agent reads when it decides whether to hand a task to that subagent. The coordinator in this scenario is behaving as designed: it compares incoming work against the descriptions it has been given. A description like "Analyzes content and extracts key findings" could reasonably match almost any research request. So the coordinator keeps spawning the document analysis subagent even when nothing has been uploaded. The fix belongs where the decision is made. Rewrite the description so it names the condition that makes the subagent relevant, such as supplied source documents, and so it clearly differs from the web search subagent.

Dynamic subagent selection is driven by descriptions, not by general requests to be careful. Telling the coordinator to be more careful about delegation gives it no new information about when document analysis applies, so it changes little. Replacing the model's choice with a hard-coded pipeline removes the coordinator's ability to analyze what each query needs. It also makes every request pay for every stage, which is the pattern the team is trying to get away from. Restricting the subagent's tools is a valid way to limit its permissions, and it may reduce unnecessary tool activity once the subagent runs. But it is not a spending limit. Real budget limits come from controls such as maxBudgetUsd, and tool restrictions do nothing about whether the subagent runs at all. Every unnecessary spawn still adds its own API calls, its own context, and its own latency to the request.

The same mechanism explains the opposite failure. A subagent that is never invoked usually has a description that does not match the way users phrase their requests. Treat descriptions as routing contracts. Keep them short so they do not fill up the coordinator's context. Put detailed working instructions in the subagent's own system prompt, which only loads when that subagent actually runs. QUESTION: The team's licensing agreement forbids retrieving content from a fixed list of restricted domains. All subagents retrieve web content solely through one fetch tool, and every subagent prompt states the rule, yet audits still find restricted-domain fetches in about 3% of research runs. What change guarantees compliance?
answers: Have the synthesis subagent rate its confidence that each source is permitted and drop uncertain ones.
Register a "PreToolUse" hook on the fetch tool that denies any call targeting a restricted domain.
Move the restricted-domain list to the top of every subagent prompt and mark it as mandatory.
Add a "PostToolUse" hook that logs any fetch from a restricted domain for later audit review.
feedbacks: A model's self-rated confidence is not a reliable measure, and this check happens after the fetch. By then the licensing breach has already happened. It also adds a second probabilistic judgment on top of the one that is already failing.

A PreToolUse hook runs as code before the tool executes, and it can return a deny decision. So a fetch to a restricted domain never happens, whatever the subagent intended. The fetch tool is the only way to retrieve content. The hook therefore changes the licensing rule from a probabilistic instruction into a deterministic check at runtime, and a guarantee requires that.

Prompt placement and emphasis can increase compliance, but compliance is still probabilistic. The rule is already in every subagent prompt and still fails in a few percent of runs. A legal obligation needs enforcement that does not depend on the model choosing to follow instructions.

PostToolUse fires only after the tool has already returned its result. When the hook runs, the restricted content has already been retrieved. Logging makes violations visible, but it cannot prevent them, and prevention is the actual requirement.
prompt.explanation:
The main distinction in this scenario is between prompt guidance and programmatic enforcement. A system prompt shapes how a subagent behaves. But every instruction in it competes with everything else in context, and the model follows it probabilistically. The 3% failure rate does not mean the wording is unclear. It is the failure rate you should expect to remain with any mechanism that depends on the model deciding to comply. When a miss creates legal exposure, the architecture needs a control that runs as code and cannot be skipped.

In the Claude Agent SDK, that control is a PreToolUse hook. The hook fires when a tool call is requested. It receives the tool_name and tool_input. It can return a permissionDecision of "deny" together with a permissionDecisionReason, which is sent back to the model so that it can choose a different source. Because the hook runs before execution, a denied fetch never happens. The SDK evaluates hooks before deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, and allow rules. If multiple hooks return different decisions, deny takes precedence, so a single deny from a correctly placed hook is final. Two practical details matter for a real guarantee. First, the hook must return a blocking decision. It must not use asynchronous hook output mode. The callback itself may be written as an async function. But output marked as async lets the agent continue immediately, and it cannot block, modify, or inject context. That mode is only suitable for side effects such as logging, metrics, or notifications. Second, the matcher must name the actual fetch tool (for example WebFetch for the built-in tool, or the specific custom or MCP tool name). It must also cover every tool that can retrieve content. A hook registered for one tool will not run if an agent reaches the same domain through another tool, such as a shell command. In this scenario the second condition is met, because the single fetch tool is the only way to retrieve content. That is why a hook on that one tool closes the gap for the whole system.

Each of the other approaches falls short in a typical way. Moving the rule to the top of every prompt and marking it mandatory is the stronger wording response. It may change the failure rate, but the rate stays above zero. A PostToolUse hook is a real hook, which makes it tempting. But it fires after a successful tool result. Its documented uses are logging, adding context, and changing what Claude sees afterward, not prevention. Asking the synthesis subagent to rate its confidence in each source adds a second probabilistic judgment after the one that is already failing. It also cannot undo a retrieval that has already happened.

As a general rule, use prompts for preferences, tone, and nuance. Use hooks whenever a rule has financial, legal, or safety consequences and must hold on every run. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: Human reviewers spot-check the final reports and find that every citation names only a document title, so verifying one claim from a 200-page filing means reading the entire document. Reviewers are rejecting reports they cannot verify. What change makes each claim verifiable?
answers: Instruct the report generator to append the most plausible page number beside each document title it cites.
Have the coordinator re-run the document analysis subagent to locate a passage whenever a reviewer questions a citation.
Require the document analysis subagent to return each finding with a quoted excerpt and its page or section location.
Pass the full text of every source document into the synthesis subagent's context so it can cite exact pages.
feedbacks: The report generator never read the source documents. Any page number it adds is a guess that looks like a verified citation. Made-up locations are worse than title-only citations. Reviewers will waste time checking pages that do not contain the claim, and they will stop trusting every other citation.

Re-running analysis on demand is a real technique. But it fixes each citation only after the report has already failed review, and it repeats expensive document processing for every question. The information was available the first time. The fix is to record it at that point instead of finding it again for each request.

The document analysis subagent is the only agent that actually reads the source. So it is the only point where the exact location of a claim can be recorded cheaply and accurately. When the excerpt and location are part of its structured output, this metadata is passed as data through synthesis and report generation. Nobody has to reconstruct it later.

Loading full documents into the synthesis stage fills its context with the long material that subagent delegation is meant to keep out. It also asks the synthesis agent to work out the locations again instead of receiving them. Because of the lost-in-the-middle effect, a synthesis agent working over many full documents becomes less reliable, not more precise.
prompt.explanation:
In a coordinator-subagent system, each stage sees less of the original material than the stage before it. The document analysis subagent reads the full text. The coordinator receives only that subagent's final report and may summarize it. The synthesis and report-generation subagents receive whatever the coordinator passes on. A detail that is not recorded in a structured field, at the stage where it is visible, will probably not reach the report. A page number or section heading is this kind of detail. It is easy to record while the document is open, and almost impossible to recover later without opening the source again.

The fix is therefore to make source location part of the subagent's output contract. Each finding should include a short quoted excerpt and the page range or section where it appears, along with the document name. With the Claude Agent SDK, you can enforce this contract by defining a JSON Schema for the subagent and passing it as output_format (Python) or outputFormat (TypeScript). The SDK validates the result and prompts the model again if it does not match. So a finding without a location field is rejected instead of being accepted without notice. Anthropic's own structured-output example has fields such as file, line, author, and date. This is the same idea applied to code instead of documents. A non-fork subagent starts with no parent history, so the requirement must be stated in the subagent's prompt or system prompt. The coordinator should also be told to map subagent output into the schema instead of paraphrasing it, because paraphrasing is where provenance (the record of where a claim came from) is usually lost.

The other approaches all try to add location information at a stage where it is more expensive and less reliable to record. Re-running the analysis subagent whenever a reviewer asks does work. But it only happens after the report has already failed, and it repeats document processing for every challenged citation. Passing full documents into the synthesis subagent brings back the long content that delegation was meant to keep separate. It also asks a later agent to work out again what the earlier agent already knew. With many long inputs, findings in the middle of that context are the ones most likely to be missed. Having the report generator add a plausible page number is the most dangerous option. The report generator never saw the source, so the result is a made-up citation. Reviewers will treat it as verified until it fails, and that damages confidence in the entire report.

As a general rule, provenance must be recorded at the source. It should never be reconstructed later. Dates, locations, methodology, and excerpts should be required fields in the structured output of the agent that reads the source directly. Every later step should keep those fields as data. See Agent SDK structured outputs and Agent SDK subagents for how output schemas and subagent context boundaries work in practice.

QUESTION: In this system, the document analysis subagent's search completed successfully but found zero matching passages. The coordinator re-ran the same query three times and then labeled the topic "source unavailable" in the report. How should the coordinator handle a successful subagent result that contains no matches?
answers: Retry the same query with exponential backoff, since zero findings usually signals a transient backend access problem.
Suppress the empty result and have the synthesis agent exclude that topic so the report contains only supported sections.
Treat the empty result as a confirmed finding, then either broaden the query or annotate the coverage gap in the report.
Ask the subagent to rate its confidence that the corpus truly contains nothing, and retry whenever that confidence is low.
feedbacks: Backoff and retry are the right response to access failures such as timeouts. An access failure is signaled by an error flag or an error payload, not by the number of results. Applying retry logic to a successful empty result wastes the tool budget. As the logs show, it also ends by wrongly reporting a real absence of evidence as a system outage.

Dropping a topic without saying so hides a coverage gap from both the synthesis agent and the reader. This works against the goal of a complete report with citations. When a subtopic has no sources, the report should show and explain that gap, not remove it from the output.

A query that completed successfully and returned nothing is information by itself: the corpus does not contain matching material for that query. The coordinator should act on this. It should rewrite the search, or record the gap honestly in the report. It should not repeat an identical query whose result is already known.

A model's self-rated confidence is not a reliable measure of whether a search was complete. It adds a probabilistic judgment to a question that the tool has already answered deterministically. Either the tool failed, or it succeeded with no matches. A confidence score does not change which of these happened.
prompt.explanation:
The main distinction in this question is between an access failure and a valid empty result. An access failure means the tool could not complete its work, for example because of a timeout, an unavailable backend, or a permission problem. A valid empty result means the tool did complete its work, and the honest answer is that nothing matched. These two outcomes need opposite responses. The only reliable way to tell them apart is a documented failure signal, not the size of the payload. In the Claude API, a client tool reports a failure by returning a tool_result with is_error set to true. A tool that succeeded but has nothing to report can correctly return an empty tool result with no error flag at all. Anthropic's own server-side web search follows the same convention. A failed search returns a web_search_tool_result_error block, while a search that found nothing returns an empty content list.

The coordinator in this scenario treated the two cases as one. Its retry rule was based on the number of results ("zero findings") instead of on the error signal. The result was predictable. A correct answer from the document analysis subagent was treated as a malfunction. Three identical queries were used to find the same fact again. The report then claimed an outage that never happened. An empty success should be treated as a finding. Once the coordinator knows that a query returned nothing, it has two useful options. It can rewrite the query, because a broader or differently worded query may find relevant passages. Or it can record the gap in the report, so readers understand which subtopics have no supporting sources. Both are correct research behaviors. Repeating the same query is not.

Each of the other approaches misreads the situation. Exponential backoff is the right tool for temporary access failures. For that reason, an error flag should trigger it, not an empty list. Self-rated confidence asks the model to doubt an outcome that the tool has already stated clearly, and a model's confidence is known to be a poor measure of completeness. Removing the topic replaces an honest, visible gap with a hidden one. This is a recognized anti-pattern in how errors move through a multi-agent system: the coordinator and the final report both need accurate information about what was found and what was not found.

See Handle tool calls for the is_error field and the empty tool result format, and Web search tool for the empty-content versus error-block distinction in server-executed search.
