QUESTION: Reports from the system described above sometimes come out incomplete, and the team cannot tell what the synthesis subagent actually received. A developer proposes giving the document analysis subagent a peer-messaging tool so it hands findings straight to synthesis. Which design should the team adopt?
answers: Keep the coordinator as the only relay, passing each subagent's final report into the synthesis prompt.
Merge document analysis and synthesis into one subagent so no inter-agent handoff is needed.
Grant the peer-messaging tool, but have each subagent append every message it sends to a shared log file.
Grant the peer-messaging tool and have the coordinator receive only the synthesis subagent's final report.
feedbacks: In the hub-and-spoke pattern, the coordinator receives every subagent's final report and decides what goes into the next subagent's prompt. Because all results pass through this one point, the team can see what synthesis received. The coordinator can also apply the same error handling to every result (for example, marking a timed-out search as a coverage gap) and control which findings go to which subagent.

Merging the two roles removes the handoff. But it also removes the context isolation and the specialized instructions that were the reason for separate subagents. The combined agent must hold long document content and synthesis reasoning in one context. This leads to attention dilution (the model's attention is spread over too much content), and it does not fix the visibility problem.

A shared log allows auditing after the fact. But it does not give back the coordinator's ability to inspect, normalize, or hold back findings before synthesis starts. It also builds custom record-keeping to imitate the visibility that the coordinator relay already provides. Error handling is still divided among the subagents.

This is the direct peer-to-peer design that is already causing problems for the team. The coordinator cannot see the handoff from document analysis to synthesis. Partial results, timeouts, and missing findings pass between subagents with no central point that can detect or mark them.
prompt.explanation:
The research system uses a hub-and-spoke topology for a reason. In the Claude Agent SDK, subagents are separate agent instances with isolated context. A non-fork subagent receives nothing from the parent conversation except the prompt string in the tool call that spawns it. When it finishes, only its final report returns to the parent. Because of this design, the coordinator is the natural channel between subagents. Unless you deliberately add a peer-messaging tool, it is the only channel. Everything the synthesis subagent knows about the search and document analysis results is what the coordinator chose to put in its prompt.

Keeping this relay in place gives three benefits at the same time. Observability: the coordinator's outgoing prompts and incoming reports are the complete record of traffic between agents. SDK mechanisms such as the SubagentStop hook and nested OpenTelemetry spans connect naturally to this parent chain. Consistent error handling: a search timeout, a corrupted PDF, or an empty result set all arrive at one place. There, the coordinator can retry, send the work elsewhere, or mark a coverage gap before synthesis begins, instead of each subagent making up its own recovery. Controlled information flow: the coordinator decides which findings each later agent sees. It removes long content that is not needed, and it keeps the mapping from each claim to its source so that provenance (the record of where a claim came from) is not lost in the handoff.

The SDK does allow peer communication when a subagent is given the SendMessage tool. But that is a deliberate choice for cases where peer messaging is the goal. The team's symptom is reports with missing content and no way to see what synthesis received. This is the result you get when the coordinator is bypassed. Logging peer messages to a file builds a weaker, custom version of the visibility the coordinator already provides. It also gives no control at the moment decisions are made. Letting the coordinator see only the synthesis report hides the handoff completely. Combining document analysis and synthesis into one agent removes the handoff problem but creates an overloaded context, which dilutes the model's attention on both jobs.

QUESTION: The team wrote a custom Messages API loop for the report-generation subagent that ends when the assistant text contains the phrase "Final report complete". Some runs stop after a mid-task section summary uses that phrase. What should determine loop termination instead?
answers: Require a more distinctive sentinel phrase in the system prompt and match it with a stricter regular expression.
Stop the loop as soon as any response includes a text block alongside its tool calls.
Continue the loop while "stop_reason" is "tool_use" and stop when the response returns "end_turn".
Cap the loop at a fixed number of iterations and treat reaching the cap as the completion signal.
feedbacks: A rarer phrase and a stricter pattern still depend on parsing natural language to decide that the work is complete. This is a documented anti-pattern. The model may leave out the phrase, write it differently, or use it again in intermediate text. So the loop stays probabilistic instead of using the signal that the protocol provides.

Assistant responses often contain text blocks and tool_use blocks together, for example a short explanation before a tool call. If the loop ends whenever text appears, it leaves pending tool calls unfinished in the middle of the task. The agent loop guidance specifically warns against this kind of completion rule.

The stop_reason field is the structured signal that the API provides for loop control. tool_use means Claude is waiting for tool results, and end_turn means Claude has finished its turn. When the loop branches on this field, it no longer depends on what the model writes in its free-form text. A section summary that repeats a phrase can no longer end the run early.

An iteration cap protects against loops that never end. It does not define when the work is done. If the cap is treated as completion, it either cuts off reports that need more tool calls, or it wastes iterations on reports that finished early. It also says nothing about whether the model actually finished.
prompt.explanation:
An agentic loop is a protocol between your harness and the model, and the protocol already includes a termination signal. Every Messages API response includes a stop_reason field. tool_use tells the harness that Claude has produced one or more tool calls and is waiting for tool_result blocks. end_turn tells the harness that Claude has finished its turn. So there is only one correct design for the loop: while stop_reason is tool_use, run the tools and send the conversation again, and when it is anything else, present the response. The harness in this scenario ignored this signal. Instead, it searched the free-form text for a sentinel phrase. The first time the model wrote that phrase in a section summary, the loop ended with the report only half built.

Rules based on text fail because assistant text is content, not control. The model writes explanations, summaries, and headings as part of doing the work, and those words can match whatever phrase you chose. A rarer phrase or a stricter regular expression does not change the kind of mechanism. It only makes accidental matches less frequent, and the loop stays probabilistic. The same reasoning rules out ending the loop whenever a response contains a text block. A single assistant message can correctly contain both text and tool_use blocks, and stopping at that point would leave the pending tool calls unfinished.

Iteration caps belong in the design, but as a safety limit, not as a definition of done. The Claude Agent SDK shows this distinction directly. max_turns has no limit by default. When the limit is reached, the SDK returns a ResultMessage whose subtype is error_max_turns. This is an explicit limit state, not a success. The SDK's own loop follows the same rule as a hand-written one. It keeps running tools until Claude produces output with no tool calls. Then it emits the final AssistantMessage and a ResultMessage that marks the end of the loop. The approach is the same whether you build on the raw API or on the SDK. Read the structured signal, use caps and budgets as safety limits, and never let the model's free-form text decide whether the harness is finished.

See Handling stop reasons and The Agent SDK agent loop for the documented termination behavior.

Read every file under "agents/" so no caller of the search client is missed.
Spawn a subagent for each top-level directory to search for callers in parallel.
Grep for "run_search" to find the wrapper's callers, then Read those files to continue the trace.
feedbacks: The one match is a wrapper, not the final user of the capability. Stopping at this point gives an incomplete and misleading answer. Every caller of the wrapper is also a code path that performs a web search, and each one must be traced.

Reading a whole directory uses context on files that have nothing to do with search. It may also miss callers that are in other directories. Grep already narrows the search to the files that matter, so reading everything is both wasteful and less reliable.

Delegating a simple content search to multiple subagents adds coordination overhead and splits the findings across separate contexts, with no benefit. A single Grep for the wrapper name answers the question directly and is faster.

A single match inside a wrapper means the real call sites are one level of indirection further away. Searching for the wrapper's name and reading the files that call it follows the chain of usage one step at a time. This is a practical use of the documented behavior of the Grep and Read tools. It builds understanding without loading the whole repository.
prompt.explanation:
Real codebases rarely call a capability from only one place. A client method such as SearchClient.search is usually wrapped by a helper function (in this case run_search) that adds retries, logging, or rate limiting. The agents that actually perform searches call the wrapper, not the client. When Grep returns one match and that match is a wrapper, the trace is not finished. It has only moved up one layer. A good next step is to Grep for the wrapper's name and Read the files that reference it. Continue to alternate between search and read until the callers are concrete agent code and not another layer of indirection.

This is how incremental exploration works. Each Grep answers a narrow question ("who references this symbol?"). Each Read confirms what the referencing code actually does. The two steps alternate until the picture is complete. The official documentation does not describe this as a named procedure. It is a practical use of how the tools are documented to behave. Grep searches file contents and can return only the matching file paths, or the matching lines with line numbers. This makes it cheap to follow a chain of symbols. Read returns the contents of a single file, so it is best used only on the files that the chain reached. Reading an entire directory does the opposite. It fills the context window with unrelated files, and it still cannot guarantee that every caller is in that directory.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. Reporting a single call site treats the wrapper as the end of the chain and produces a confident but wrong answer. Spawning one subagent per directory increases coordination cost and splits the findings, when a direct Grep call is faster and enough. Anthropic's prompting guidance specifically warns against overusing subagents for this kind of code exploration. QUESTION: The report generator subagent needs to fix one citation block in a generated Markdown report. Edit fails because the block appears in five identical sections, and even when the match text is extended with surrounding lines, it still matches more than once. What should the subagent do next?
answers: Call Edit again with "replace_all" set to true so the uniqueness requirement no longer applies.
Retry the identical Edit call a few times with backoff in case the match failure is transient.
Switch to Bash and patch the targeted lines in the report with a sed command.
Read the full file, apply the change within that content, then Write the complete updated file.
feedbacks: The replace_all option changes every occurrence of the old_string text. The task is to correct only one of the five citation blocks. Using replace_all would change four sections that should stay as they are.

A non-unique match is a deterministic result of the file's content. It is not a temporary fault. Repeating the same Edit call with the same old_string will fail in the same way every time, and it wastes turns.

Bash with sed can technically change the file. But it replaces a controlled file operation with a fragile stream edit, and that edit must still pick out one occurrence among identical blocks. The dedicated file tools are preferred. Bash should be used only for tasks those tools cannot do.

When no unique match text exists, the documented fallback is to load the whole file with Read, make the change in that content, and overwrite the file with Write. This avoids the exact-match requirement completely and still meets the read-before-write constraints. The cost is that the entire file must be sent.
prompt.explanation:
The Edit tool in Claude Code performs exact string replacement. It takes an old_string and a new_string, and the old text must appear exactly once in the file unless replace_all is set. This design is deliberate. Exact, unique matching makes each edit small, easy to audit, and safe to apply without the model holding the entire file in context. That is why Edit is the preferred tool for partial changes to existing files. The usual fix for a duplicate match is to make the match text longer by adding surrounding lines until it is unique. The scenario says this has already been tried and the surrounding text is also identical. So the matching mechanism has no way to say which block is meant.

At this point, the correct step is the Read then Write fallback. Read returns the full file contents with line numbers. The subagent produces the corrected version of the whole document. Write then overwrites the file with the complete content it is given. Write does not append or merge. It replaces the entire file. This is why Read must come first: the model needs the full, current text to reproduce everything that should stay unchanged, and a partial read is not enough. Claude Code also applies read-before-overwrite constraints to existing files. There are limited exceptions for newer models when reading the file would not require a permission prompt. A file that was seen only through a partial view must be read in any case. The cost of this fallback is that the whole file passes through the context window twice. So it is reserved for cases where Edit's precise mechanism cannot work. For very large files, a single Read may be split into pages or limited in size. The subagent should therefore confirm that it has the complete content, not a partial view, before it writes.

Setting replace_all to true is a real option, but it exists for the opposite situation, where every occurrence should change. In this scenario it would change four correct sections without any warning. Retrying the same Edit call treats a deterministic content condition as if it were a temporary service error, which it is not. Switching to Bash and sed avoids the file tools instead of using them. It still has to tell identical blocks apart, it produces no structured result for the agent to verify, and it bypasses the file tools that Claude Code was built to use. See the Claude Code tools reference for the documented behavior of Read, Edit, and Write.

QUESTION: The web search subagent returns 25 sources. The coordinator then invokes the document analysis subagent (a standard subagent, not a fork) with the prompt "analyze the documents found in the previous step," and the analysis subagent replies that no documents were provided. How should the coordinator fix this handoff?
answers: Add a system prompt instruction telling the analysis subagent to review the coordinator's earlier tool results before starting.
Retry the delegation with firmer wording insisting the subagent locate the documents identified in the previous phase.
Set the search findings as the analysis subagent's "initialPrompt" in its definition so they load automatically on invocation.
Summarize the search phase findings and include the source list in the delegation prompt that spawns the analysis subagent.
feedbacks: An instruction cannot give the subagent access to data that is not in its context. A non-fork subagent cannot see the parent's tool results. If you tell it to review them, it will again report that it has nothing to analyze.

Stronger wording does not change what information the subagent has. The failure is that the content was never handed over, not that the subagent is unwilling to follow instructions. Repeating the request more forcefully leaves the same empty context in place.

In the Agent SDK, the initialPrompt field of an AgentDefinition is submitted automatically only when that agent runs as the main thread agent. It is ignored when the agent is invoked as a subagent. So the search findings would still never reach the analysis subagent.

A non-fork subagent starts with a new, empty context window. It does not inherit the coordinator's conversation history or its earlier tool results. The only task-specific content it receives from the parent is the delegation prompt. So the coordinator must reduce the search phase to its key findings and put the source list directly in that prompt.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent is a separate agent instance with its own context window. A standard, non-fork subagent starts fresh. It receives its own system prompt, the CLAUDE.md files that apply, and the task prompt that the parent writes when it calls the Agent tool. It does not receive the parent's conversation history or the parent's earlier tool results. Only forked subagents copy the conversation so far, and this scenario clearly uses a non-fork subagent. This isolation is deliberate. It keeps long search output, file reads, and intermediate reasoning out of the coordinator's context window, and only the subagent's final report comes back to the parent.

The other side of this isolation is that context must be passed explicitly. The documented pattern for chained phases works like this: one subagent finishes and returns results to the coordinator, and the coordinator then writes the relevant context into the next subagent's delegation prompt. A phrase like "the documents found in the previous step" refers to nothing inside a fresh context window. The fix is for the coordinator to summarize the key findings of the search phase (which sources were found, why they matter, and any constraints it discovered) and to include the concrete source list in the prompt that spawns the analysis subagent. Summarizing before the handoff also keeps the delegation prompt focused. The analysis subagent then uses its own context on the documents, not on the coordinator's search transcript.

The incorrect approaches all assume a channel that does not exist. The initialPrompt field in an AgentDefinition is a real setting. But it is submitted automatically only when that agent runs as the main thread agent, and it is ignored when the agent is invoked as a subagent, so it is not a handoff mechanism. A system prompt instruction to review the coordinator's earlier tool results cannot show the subagent data that it never received. Firmer wording on a retry changes the tone, not the content, and the context stays empty. In every case the missing piece is the same: the parent must put the findings in the delegation prompt.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: A developer paused an Agent SDK session in which the agent had mapped how the synthesis subagent assembles citations. Most of those source files have since been refactored. Which TWO approaches keep the continued work from relying on stale analysis? (Select TWO.)
answers: Resume the session and have the agent rate its confidence in the earlier analysis before continuing the work.
Register a "SessionStart" hook that injects the list of recently changed files into the agent's context on resume.
Resume the session unchanged, because the agent's earlier file reads are refreshed automatically from disk when it loads.
Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of prior findings and a note of which files were refactored.
feedbacks: A model's self-rated confidence is not a reliable measure of whether its earlier observations are still true. The agent cannot know that the files were refactored unless someone tells it or it reads them again. This option adds a judgment step but does not provide the missing fact about what changed.

The SessionStart event fires when a session starts or is resumed. Its documented uses include loading recent codebase changes into context. When the hook returns the list of changed files as additionalContext, the model sees this information before its first turn. It then knows which earlier reads it must do again.

A session stores the conversation history, including old tool results. It does not store a live view of the filesystem. Nothing reads the files again on resume. The agent would reason from the pre-refactor contents it saw earlier, unless something tells it that those files changed.

Most of the analyzed files have changed, so the saved tool results in the old session describe code that no longer exists. Resuming would carry that outdated evidence forward. A new session that receives a short summary of what was learned, plus a clear statement of which files changed, lets the agent keep the useful conclusions while it reads the current code again.
prompt.explanation:
An Agent SDK session is a saved conversation history: the prompts, the tool calls, the tool results, and the responses. It is not a snapshot of the working tree. When you resume, the agent gets back everything it previously read and concluded, word for word. But the files on disk may have changed since then. This difference is the whole problem with resuming after code changes. The agent has strong, specific evidence in its context about how the synthesis subagent built citations, and that evidence is now wrong. If nothing changes, the agent will reason confidently from the old file contents, because nothing inside the transcript looks different.

Two responses fix this problem. The first is a decision rule: when most of the earlier tool results are outdated, start a new session instead of resuming. That is the situation in this scenario, because most of the mapped files were refactored. Give the new session a structured summary of what was learned and a clear note of which files were refactored. The agent keeps the overall understanding that took time to build. Every claim about the current code is worked out again from new reads instead of being inherited from outdated ones. Resuming is the better choice only when the earlier context is still mostly valid and the changes are small enough to point to directly.

The second response is automation: a SessionStart hook. This event runs when a session starts or is resumed, and its documented uses include loading recent codebase changes. Whatever the hook returns as additionalContext is placed in the model's context before its first turn. So a hook that lists the files changed since the session was last active tells the agent which earlier reads to redo. This matters because context that hooks add during a session is replayed on resume, not computed again. That is why the refresh belongs in a hook that actually runs again at resume time. Note that systemMessage only shows text to the user. The model sees additionalContext.

The incorrect approaches fail for related reasons. Resuming unchanged assumes a refresh mechanism that does not exist: file reads are not run again when a session loads. Asking the agent to rate its own confidence adds a step but not the missing fact. The model cannot know that files were refactored by examining its own reasoning, and self-rated confidence is a poor measure of whether earlier observations are still true. In both cases, the fix is to provide the information about what changed, or to redo the analysis. Do not trust the outdated transcript.

See Agent SDK sessions for what a session persists and Claude Code hooks for SessionStart behavior on resume.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: In this system, the synthesis subagent has an MCP tool "query_findings" that returns findings with source attribution from the shared store, but its description reads only "Queries findings" and documents no parameters. The subagent instead Greps the raw scratchpad files. Which TWO changes most directly fix this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Add a blanket system prompt rule telling the subagent to always prefer MCP tools over built-in tools.
Reorder the tool definitions so the MCP tool appears before Grep in the list sent to the model.
Drop Grep from the synthesis subagent's tool list so only role-relevant tools remain available.
Expand the description with the query parameter's expected format and example queries the tool should handle.
feedbacks: A general preference rule in the system prompt is probabilistic guidance that the model may ignore. It also does not fix the reason the MCP tool looks unattractive to the model. Tool selection happens where the model reads the tool descriptions. Broad "always use" instructions are a form of over-prompting. They can also push the model toward the MCP tool in cases where a built-in tool is the right choice.

The position of a tool in the list is not a documented or reliable way to control selection, so reordering leaves the real problem unsolved. The model still sees a vague description with no parameter guidance next to a fully capable Grep tool. It will keep choosing the tool it understands.

Tool availability is an architectural control. If a built-in tool is present, the model can select it or misuse it. The synthesis role is to write and combine attributed findings, not to search raw files. When the subagent's tool set matches its role, the competing path is gone completely. The model no longer has to choose between the MCP tool and a built-in tool that its role does not need.

Tool descriptions are the main way the model decides whether and how to call a tool. A two-word description with no parameter guidance gives the model little reason to call query_findings, and little information about how to do it. Documenting the input format and example queries shows the model how to write the calls. The MCP tool then becomes a usable choice, not an unclear one that the model avoids.
prompt.explanation:
When a subagent uses a built-in tool such as Grep instead of a more capable MCP tool, the model is making a selection decision with the information it has at that moment. That information is almost entirely the set of tool definitions it can see. Anthropic describes the tool description as by far the most important factor in tool performance. It recommends that the description explain what the tool does, when to use it, what each parameter means, and what it returns. A description that says only "Queries findings", with no parameter guidance, does not tell the model how to call the tool. It also does not say why the tool is better than searching the scratchpad files. So the model falls back to the tool it already understands.

Adding the query parameter's format and concrete example queries to the description fixes the how. The model now knows what a valid call looks like and what kinds of requests the tool is meant for. The same principle makes input formats and example queries effective when requests go to the wrong one of two overlapping tools. In this scenario, the overlap is between an MCP tool and a built-in tool. The second fix is architectural, not descriptive. Each subagent should get only the tools its role needs. A synthesis agent's job is to combine attributed findings into clear output, not to search raw files. Removing Grep from its tool set removes the competing path deterministically. This is why availability controls are the documented complement to good descriptions when a built-in tool keeps being chosen.

The other approaches fall short for related reasons. A general system prompt rule to always prefer MCP tools is probabilistic guidance added on top of a tool that is still not explained. Broad "always use" wording also tends to make the model call the MCP tool too often, including in cases where a built-in tool is appropriate. Reordering tool definitions depends on position effects, and these are not a reliable mechanism. The model still sees the same vague description next to a Grep tool it understands well. The reliable pattern has two parts. Make the MCP tool easy to understand through its description. And when the role does not need the built-in alternative, remove that alternative from the subagent's tool set.

See Define tools for description best practices and Claude Code MCP for how MCP tools are shown to the model.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: The coordinator chooses between two summarizing tools: "summarize_source", run by the web-search agent, and "summarize_document", run by the document agent. Both tools have the description "summarizes a source and returns key points." Requests to summarize uploaded whitepapers often go to "summarize_source". Which TWO changes most directly resolve the misrouting? (Select TWO.)
answers: Add few-shot routing examples to the coordinator prompt showing uploads going to the document agent.
Insert a pre-routing classifier that inspects each request for file references before the coordinator delegates.
Rename the web-search agent's tool to "summarize_web_page" so its name no longer mirrors the document tool.
Rewrite both descriptions to state when each applies, such as fetched URLs versus uploaded files.
feedbacks: Few-shot examples can change behavior somewhat. But they add token overhead to every request, and the identical tool definitions stay in place. The root cause is that the tool interfaces overlap. Examples only hide that problem, and their effect is probabilistic.

A classifier adds a new component to make up for a defect in the tool definitions, instead of fixing the definitions. This is over-engineering. Once the tools have clear names and descriptions, the coordinator can route correctly without an extra layer.

The two names differ by one generic word, and both suggest the same capability. So the name gives the coordinator nothing to tell them apart. A web-specific name removes this conflict at the point where the model reads the tool definitions.

Descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose a tool. Identical descriptions give it nothing to tell the tools apart. Stating when each tool should and should not be used directly removes the ambiguity that causes the wrong agent to be selected.
prompt.explanation:
When a coordinator delegates to subagents, it is in effect choosing among tool definitions. Claude makes that choice based on the user request and on each tool's name and description. In this scenario, the two names differ only by a generic noun, and the descriptions are identical word for word. The model has no signal that tells the tools apart. It will pick one based on how similar the words look to the request, and that produces the inconsistent routing seen in this scenario. The documented diagnosis for selecting the wrong tool is description ambiguity. The documented fix is to make the definitions clearer, so that they differ by when each tool applies, not only by what it does.

The two changes that fix the root cause are both in the tool interface itself. Renaming the web-search tool to something like summarize_web_page removes the near-duplicate name. This follows the broader practice of making names show their service or source, so that selection stays unambiguous as the number of tools grows. Rewriting the descriptions to state when each tool applies ("use for pages retrieved from a URL; do not use for uploaded files" versus "use for uploaded PDFs, Word documents, and spreadsheets") gives the model the distinguishing information it reads when it selects a tool. Anthropic calls detailed descriptions the single most important factor in tool performance. It recommends that they cover what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, and its caveats.

The other approaches treat the symptom, not the cause. Few-shot routing examples in the coordinator prompt cost tokens on every call, and they only change probabilities while the overlapping definitions remain. A pre-routing classifier builds new infrastructure to work around a defect that a few sentences of description would remove. The classifier also becomes another component to maintain and tune. As a general rule, when tool selection is wrong, fix the names and descriptions first. That change has the most effect for the lowest cost.

See Define tools for description best practices and naming guidance, and Troubleshooting tool use for the diagnosis of wrong-tool selection.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: Research runs take several hours. When the coordinator process crashes midway, the restarted run repeats web searches that had already finished and discards partial document analysis. Which design lets the coordinator pick up where the run stopped?
answers: Wrap the entire pipeline in an automatic retry with backoff so a crashed run restarts itself from the beginning without operator action.
Resume the coordinator's saved session on restart so that every subagent automatically continues from the last tool result that it had recorded.
Give each subagent a larger context budget so a single long-running pass finishes the entire pipeline before any crash can interrupt it.
Export each subagent's structured state to a known location, and load it as a manifest the coordinator feeds into subsequent subagent prompts.
feedbacks: Automatic restart only automates the problem described in the scenario. Every retry runs the web searches again, even though they already succeeded, and throws away the analysis that was in progress. Retries with backoff are the right response to temporary tool failures. But they do not keep completed work when the process crashes.

A saved session holds the coordinator's transcript, not the application state of the pipeline. Subagents do not inherit or share that transcript. Each subagent starts fresh with only the prompt string it is given. So resuming the coordinator does not restore partly completed document analysis, and it does not pass earlier search results to the next phase.

A larger context budget does nothing to prevent a process crash. All progress stays in memory, and that memory is lost when the process dies. Context size controls how much a subagent can hold in one conversation. It does not control whether its results are saved for a later run.

When each subagent writes its status, findings, coverage, and gaps to a known location, its progress becomes durable application state that survives a process crash. On restart, the coordinator reads the manifest and sees which phases are complete. It then passes those results explicitly into the prompts of the subagents that still need to run. Finished work is reused instead of repeated.
prompt.explanation:
The main distinction in this design is between conversation state and application state. An Agent SDK session records the prompt, tool calls, tool results, and responses of one agent. The SDK writes that transcript to local disk and can resume it later. A session does not hold the pipeline's own record of progress: which research phases are complete, what each subagent found, and which topics are still not covered. A crash in a research run that takes several hours is a loss of application state. So the recovery mechanism has to be built at the application layer.

Structured state exports give the coordinator that layer. Each subagent writes a small structured record when it finishes, or at useful checkpoints. The record contains its status, the queries it ran, key findings with their sources, the topics it covered, and the gaps it noticed. The coordinator keeps a manifest that maps each phase to a state such as completed, in progress, or not started. On restart, it loads the manifest, skips completed phases, and builds the next subagent prompt from the stored findings. This last step matters because subagents do not inherit the coordinator's context. A new subagent sees only the prompt string it receives, so recovered results must be placed into that prompt deliberately. The same structured records are also useful later in synthesis, for provenance and for marking coverage gaps. So the recovery design is useful even when nothing crashes.

Resuming the coordinator's session is the tempting alternative. The SDK does save transcripts durably, and resume with a tracked session ID will bring back the coordinator's conversation. But the documentation clearly states that sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem or the surrounding application. It also states that resuming a subagent requires resuming the same session with that subagent's own agent identifier and defining the agent again. Nothing in that mechanism rebuilds a half-finished document analysis or passes search results to the next phase. The coordinator would still have to decide what to redo, and without a manifest it has no reliable record to base that decision on. Anthropic's own guidance for work across hosts and over long periods says the same thing: record results, decisions, and progress as structured state, and pass them into a fresh prompt.

The other two options are common types of wrong answers. Wrapping the pipeline in retries treats a crash like a temporary tool error. Retries are appropriate for a timed-out search, but when the whole process restarts they only run completed work again. Enlarging the context budget confuses how much one conversation can hold with whether anything survives when the process ends. A bigger window loses just as much when the process dies. See Agent SDK sessions for what resume does and does not restore, and Agent SDK subagents for why recovered state must be passed explicitly into subagent prompts.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: Reports from the system described above on broad topics such as "autonomous vehicle regulation" consistently cover only United States federal rules; coordinator logs show it assigned three subtasks, all within that one area. Which change most directly fixes this coverage gap?
answers: Instruct the synthesis subagent to write additional sections for any regions the gathered findings omit.
Revise the coordinator prompt to map the topic's full scope into distinct subtasks before delegating.
Raise the web search subagent's result limit so each assigned query returns more sources.
Move the synthesis subagent to a larger context window so it can retain every finding.
feedbacks: The synthesis subagent can only work from the findings the coordinator passes to it. No findings about other jurisdictions exist, because no subagent researched them. If it is asked to write those sections anyway, it will produce content without citations, based on the model's general knowledge instead of on researched, sourced material. That defeats the purpose of the system.

The coverage gap starts earlier in the pipeline. The coordinator split a broad topic into three subtasks that were all inside one jurisdiction, so no subagent was ever assigned the missing areas. The documented fix for delegation that leaves gaps is to have the coordinator map the full scope of the topic and divide it into distinct subtasks with clear boundaries. This fixes the problem at the point where it happens.

More results per query would give deeper coverage of the subtasks that were actually assigned, and all of them were about United States federal rules. The search subagent carried out its assignments correctly. Returning more sources on the same narrow subtasks does not add the jurisdictions that the coordinator never asked about.

Context capacity is not the limiting factor. The synthesis subagent is not losing findings that it received. The findings for other regions were never produced. A larger context window helps with information loss while results are combined, and that is a different failure from narrow task decomposition.
prompt.explanation:
In a hub-and-spoke research system, the coordinator's task decomposition is the one decision that sets what the rest of the system can possibly find. Every subagent works with isolated context and does only the subtask it is given. It cannot see the original user query except for what the coordinator put in its prompt. It also cannot notice that the other subagents are all working on the same small part of the topic. When the coordinator divides "autonomous vehicle regulation" into three subtasks that are all inside United States federal rules, the search, analysis, and synthesis subagents each succeed at their assignments. The report is still incomplete, and nothing reports the gap. This is why the logs are the diagnostic clue. When every later stage works correctly and the report is still missing part of the scope, the cause is the decomposition, not any worker.

Anthropic's write-up on its own multi-agent research system describes this failure directly. The lead agent must give each subagent an objective, an output format, guidance on sources, and clear task boundaries. Without these, subagents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find the information they need. In Anthropic's example, a vague delegation to "research the semiconductor shortage" led one subagent to study a 2021 automotive crisis while two others both studied current supply chains. That is the same unbalanced coverage seen in this scenario. The fix is to make the coordinator first reason about the full scope of the topic. It should then divide the scope into subtasks that do not overlap, and choose the number of subtasks based on how broad the question is instead of always using a small fixed number. You can write the coordinator prompt in terms of coverage goals and quality criteria. You can also add a refinement pass, in which the coordinator checks the synthesized findings for gaps and sends out follow-up subtasks. Both keep the fix at the level where the error was made.

Each of the other approaches changes a component that is not broken. The synthesis subagent only sees what the coordinator passes on. If it is told to write sections for the missing regions, the coverage gap is replaced by content that has no citations and was never researched. Raising the search subagent's result limit gives more depth on the narrow subtasks it already had, but it does not make them broader. A larger context window for synthesis fixes a different failure, the loss of findings while results are combined. In this scenario, the findings were never gathered. In a coordinator-subagent architecture, the breadth of the research is set when the coordinator delegates. Every later agent inherits any gaps in the coordinator's decomposition.

Further reading: How we built our multi-agent research system and Subagents in the SDK.

SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

QUESTION: The extraction agent calls a vendor lookup tool for every invoice in a session; each call returns more than 40 fields, but extraction needs only three. Accuracy drops by the twelfth invoice. Which TWO changes address this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to disregard any vendor fields that are not relevant to the extraction.
Trim the vendor lookup response to only the fields the extraction step actually uses before it enters context.
Enable server-side context editing so older tool results are cleared once a configured token threshold is exceeded.
Mark the vendor lookup results with "cache_control" so the repeated fields stop counting against the context window.
feedbacks: An instruction to ignore fields does not remove them from context. Every irrelevant field still uses tokens and competes for the model's attention on each turn. The accuracy loss is caused by what fills the context window, not by a lack of guidance about which fields are relevant.

Tool results are added to the conversation and sent again with every later request. So a 40-field record uses context on each turn, no matter how few fields matter. Returning only the useful fields stops the growth at its source. This is the documented guidance for designing tool responses.

Context editing with the tool-result clearing strategy removes older tool results from the history once the threshold is crossed. It replaces them with placeholder text. This directly reduces the accumulated tool output that is filling the extraction context, while recent results stay available.

Prompt caching reduces what you pay for repeated tokens. But cached content still takes up its full space in the context window. The 40-field records would keep accumulating and would reduce accuracy in the same way as before, only at a lower price.
prompt.explanation:
The Messages API is stateless. Every request carries the full transcript, including each earlier assistant tool_use block and every tool_result block that the application added. So a vendor record with more than forty fields does not cost its tokens only once. It is sent again on every later turn of the session, and a dozen invoices means a dozen such records piled up in the context window. Anthropic's tool-use guidance clearly states that accumulated tool results consume the context window, and that long-running agents can use it all up before they finish. That is why tool outputs grow disproportionately to their relevance (they grow much faster than their usefulness) is listed as a reliability risk, not as a small note about cost.

The two effective responses address the problem at different layers. Trimming the tool response to the three fields that the extraction step uses is the fix at the source. Tool-design best practice says that responses should contain only the information the next step needs, because large responses waste context and make it harder for Claude to find what matters. In a Claude Agent SDK pipeline, this is usually done in a PostToolUse hook or in the MCP tool itself. Server-side context editing is the fix later in the process. The clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy clears older tool results once a configured threshold is exceeded and replaces them with placeholder text. By default it keeps the tool call parameters, unless clear_tool_inputs is set. Together, the two changes reduce what enters the context window and limit how much of it stays there.

The other options look reasonable, but they misunderstand what takes up context. Applying cache_control to tool results lowers the price of repeated tokens. But Anthropic clearly documents that prompt caching is not context reduction. Cached prefixes still fill the context window, and the loss of accuracy continues as before. A system prompt instruction to ignore irrelevant fields is a probabilistic hint added on top of the same overloaded context. The fields are still there, still use tokens, and still compete for attention. The instruction treats the symptom and leaves the cause in place.

SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

QUESTION: In this system, the extraction call also rates its own confidence for each field. However, fields that later turn out to be wrong get confidence above 0.9 just as often as correct fields, so almost nothing is routed to reviewers. What change makes the confidence signal usable for routing?
answers: Ask the extraction call to critique its own draft output and revise each confidence value before returning the result.
Run the extraction three times and average the three confidence values reported for each field.
Run a separate verification pass in a fresh instance that checks each field against the source and assigns confidence.
Lower the routing threshold so that any field below 0.95 confidence is sent to a human reviewer.
feedbacks: Self-critique inside the same call keeps the reasoning that produced the value. So the model tends to confirm its own decisions instead of questioning them. The confidence would still be a self-assessment with the same bias. That bias is the reason wrong fields currently get scores as high as correct ones.

Averaging repeated self-ratings reduces random variation between runs. But it does not correct a systematic tendency to report high confidence on wrong values. Three uncalibrated scores averaged together are still uncalibrated. The extra calls add cost without improving routing.

A verification pass that runs without the extractor's reasoning context must find evidence in the source for each value. The confidence it produces shows whether the data is actually supported, not whether the generator felt sure. When the judgement is separate from the generation step, the routing stage gets a signal that differs between correct and incorrect fields.

Moving the threshold does not make the numbers carry more information. If wrong and correct fields both have scores above 0.9, a stricter cutoff still cannot separate them. It mostly changes how many extractions reviewers see, not which ones need attention.
prompt.explanation:
A confidence value in an extraction schema is a model-produced field. It is not a probability produced by the API. Structured output guarantees that the JSON can be parsed and matches the schema. It says nothing about whether the number in the confidence field matches reality. When the same call that produced a value also rates how sure it is, the model makes the rating with all the reasoning that led to the value. A model is unlikely to question a decision it has just justified to itself. This is the same self-review limitation that makes an author a poor reviewer of their own pull request. It shows up as scores that are high for every field, whether the field is correct or not.

The pattern that produces a usable signal is a separate verification pass. A fresh instance receives the source document and the extracted values, but not the extractor's reasoning. For each field, it must find the supporting passage before it assigns confidence. Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends this evidence-first check: ask the model to find a supporting quote for each claim, and to withdraw claims it cannot support. Confidence that is based on whether evidence was found behaves differently for correct and incorrect fields, and a routing stage needs that difference. This matches the broader guidance to separate coverage from filtering. Let the extraction step report everything, and let a later pass judge and rank the results. The verification pass reduces miscalibration but does not remove it completely. So the resulting scores should still be checked against labeled examples before the thresholds are fixed.

The other approaches do not change the nature of the signal. When the extraction call critiques its own draft, the judgement stays inside the generation context, so the same confirmation bias remains. Lowering the routing threshold only changes how many extractions reviewers see. If wrong and correct fields both score above 0.9, no cutoff can separate them. Averaging three self-ratings reduces random variation, but the systematic overconfidence stays, and the cost is three times higher.

The failing extractions already contain a total. The problem is that it does not match the line items. Making fields required fixes missing values, not wrong ones. It can also push the model to make up values when a document really does not contain the information.

Strict tool use makes the guarantee stronger that tool input matches the schema, including types, required fields, and enums. The scenario shows that the output already matches the structure. The problem is that values that match the schema are wrong, and no schema constraint can detect that.

Defining an extraction as a tool whose input_schema describes the desired output is the most reliable way to get JSON from Claude that can be parsed and matches the schema. A JSON schema fixes the shape of the data, not whether it is true. A schema can require that total is a number and that customer is a string. These are semantic errors, and they are what the finance team is seeing. The pattern for that remaining class is a validation-retry loop. Code validates the extraction against business rules: totals must match the line items, dates must be in order, and each field must hold the expected kind of entity. When validation fails, the system prompts the model again with the original document, the previous extraction, and the specific error. A design that works well with this is to have the schema record both a stated_total and a calculated_total, with a conflict_detected flag. Then differences in the source document itself are reported instead of being resolved without notice. In this scenario, the information does not exist in the document. No number of retries can find a termination date that was never written. Each retry also still ends with a required field that must be filled.

A required string field gives the model no valid way to say that the information is missing. So it fills the field with an invented value to satisfy the schema. When the schema allows null, the model has an honest, valid answer for a missing clause. Downstream code can then handle null deterministically instead of trusting a made-up date.

This keeps the invented value and asks the model to grade its own invention. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated in these cases in particular. It also adds a second field that the model must always fill, instead of removing the pressure to fill the first one.

The schema still requires a string in every extraction. So the instruction and the schema ask for opposite things, and the model must put something in the field. Prompt guidance is probabilistic. prompt.explanation:

The model produces well-formed JSON with the declared fields and types, so JSON.parse() failures and missing-field errors mostly disappear. That is why schema design is part of extraction reliability. Fields that may really be missing from the source should be nullable (for example, a type array of string and null). The model can then return null instead of a believable invented value. The same reasoning leads to related patterns. Add an "unclear" enum value for cases where a classification cannot be made with confidence. Add an "other" enum value together with a free-text detail field, so that categories outside the list are not forced into the wrong category without notice. Each of these gives the model an honest answer that is still schema-valid. For downstream systems, this is much better than a confident wrong value that passes every check.

Fixing the schema removes the cause, instead of trying to detect the symptom.

feedbacks: A small uniform random sample consists mostly of the common document types. It will rarely find a rare document type or field with a high error rate. It also assumes that the overall number can be trusted, and that is the assumption that must be tested first.

Schema validation guarantees structural correctness, such as valid JSON, required fields, and correct types. It says nothing about whether the extracted values are right. A completely valid document can still contain wrong amounts or dates. So this does not show that review can be reduced.

An overall figure of 97% can hide a segment that performs much worse, such as one document layout or one field that often fails. Checking accuracy for each document type and each field confirms that performance is actually stable everywhere before any review is removed. This check is required before automation is safe.

Self-rated confidence is a poor measure, because the model can be confident and wrong. An uncalibrated score has no proven relationship to real error rates. Confidence scores become useful only after they are calibrated against labeled data and after accuracy has been verified for each segment.
prompt.explanation:
An aggregate accuracy metric is an average over a mix of very different inputs. Suppose a corpus is 90% clean, standardized forms and 10% scanned legacy contracts. It can report 97% overall while the legacy contracts fail 40% of the time. If human review is removed because of the overall number, the remaining errors are concentrated in the segment that was never measured separately. Breaking the results down by document type and by field turns one number that hides the details into a grid. The grid shows where the system is reliable and where it is not. Anthropic's evaluation guidance makes this concrete. An eval set should match the real-world distribution of inputs and should deliberately include edge cases. Success criteria should be specific and measurable, not a single headline score. Field-level breakdowns also show patterns that document-level scoring misses. Once the accuracy of each segment is known, the team can add calibrated field-level confidence thresholds and stratified sampling to keep watching for new error patterns. But these tools are added on top of the segment analysis. They do not replace it.

Each of the incorrect approaches skips this verification. Relying on the model's self-reported confidence replaces measured accuracy with an uncalibrated signal. A model that is wrong on a hard document type is often wrong with full confidence. Strict schema validation is valuable. But the Structured outputs documentation clearly states that it guarantees valid JSON, required fields, and field types, not that the values are correct compared to the source document. A small uniform random audit is cheap. But it samples each type in proportion to how often it appears. So a rare document type with a high error rate may add zero items to the sample, and its errors go undetected.

As a general rule, decide on automation for each segment separately, never for the whole corpus at once. Switch to a model with a larger context window so the entire packet is processed comfortably in one pass.

Conflicting values for the same field show that no step explicitly compares the documents. A separate pass for each document gives every document the same level of attention. A dedicated reconciliation pass is the right place to compare the income figures and flag the difference.

The packet already fits in the context window, because the call completes. The problem is how attention is divided across many documents, not whether they fit. A larger window does not make a single pass examine each document in equal depth.

Validation-retry loops fix format and structural errors, such as a badly formatted date or a field in the wrong place. In this scenario, the output is schema-valid. The problems are missing detail and contradictory values, and a schema error message cannot describe or correct them.

prompt.explanation:
When a single prompt asks Claude to extract from many documents at once, its attention is divided across too many documents. The model tends to analyze some documents carefully and only skim others. It also never performs an explicit comparison step. So the same field (an applicant's income) can be taken from two documents with different values, and nobody notices. This attention dilution comes from how a single pass divides its effort across a large input with many different kinds of documents. It is not a capacity problem, so it continues even when the packet fits easily in the context window.

The fix is to split the work into focused passes that you implement in your own pipeline. Run one pass per document, and have each pass produce its own schema-conformant extraction. Then run a separate integration pass whose only job is work across documents. For example, it reconciles the income figures, checks that totals agree, and sets a conflict_detected flag when sources disagree. Each per-document pass starts with a clean, narrow context. This is the same reason Anthropic recommends delegating self-contained research to subagents. With isolated context, each unit of work does not compete for attention with everything else, and the parent then combines the summaries that come back. The Subagents documentation describes this pattern of independent investigations followed by synthesis. The context window guide explains how separate context windows keep large reads from filling up the main conversation.

Each of the incorrect approaches targets a different problem. A larger context window helps the input fit, but it does not improve focus. Majority voting over three diluted passes adds agreement on top of unreliable detections. It removes real values that appeared only once, and it hides the income conflict instead of reporting it. But it has nothing to send back when the output is syntactically valid and the defect is uneven coverage. Retries cannot provide the attention that the first pass never gave.

Add "minimum" and "maximum" keywords to the schema so the API rejects any value outside the expected range.
Validate parsed values in code afterward, because a schema-conformant response can still contain un-normalized numbers.

Numeric constraints such as minimum and maximum are among the JSON Schema features that Anthropic's structured outputs do not support. Sending them directly can cause a 400 error instead of being enforced. Even when an SDK helper moves them into the descriptions, the API does not check the range of values. On a successful response, structured output produces well-formed JSON whose fields have the declared types. It does not guarantee that the values in those fields are correct or normalized. Anthropic's prompting guidance is to be specific about output constraints and to put these instructions in the prompt or in the field descriptions, where the model actually reads them.

That is a problem for instructions, not for types.

A required, non-nullable string forces the model to provide some value even when the document has none, so the model guesses. Declaring the field as a string or null gives the model an honest way to report that the value is missing. The added instruction tells it to use null when there is no evidence in the source.

The prompt and the schema now directly conflict. The schema still requires a string for every required field, so the model has no compliant way to follow the instruction. Prompt wording alone cannot override a structural requirement that only accepts a value.

Retry with error feedback works for format and structural mistakes that the model can correct by reading the document again. It does not help when the required information is missing from the source. Every retry faces the same impossible requirement and produces another guess.
prompt.explanation:
Schema-driven extraction has two levels of strength. Two methods constrain the output to the schema: JSON outputs provided through output_config.format, and tool calls made with strict tool use enabled ("strict": true on the tool definition). With these, the shape of the result is guaranteed: valid syntax, correct types, and every field listed in required present. A plain tool input_schema without strict mode strongly guides the model toward that shape, but it does not fully guarantee required fields and types. In neither case does the schema guarantee that the values are true. The schema is a contract that the model tries to satisfy on every call. When a document has nothing that can fill a required field, the model resolves the conflict by inferring a value that looks reasonable. Anthropic documents this behavior: when required parameters cannot be found, Claude may guess them instead of leaving them out. Under strict enforcement, a guessed value is the only compliant option.

The safe design for production is to let the schema express uncertainty. A field that a source may really lack should be declared with a union type such as "type": ["string", "null"], or left out of required when the downstream contract allows the value to be missing. Pair this with a prompt instruction to return null when the document contains no evidence. This gives the model an option that is both compliant and honest. The same principle is behind adding an unclear enum value, or an other option with a detail string. Optional and union types make the grammar more complex under strict enforcement. So make only the fields that are really uncertain nullable, not every property.

The other approaches leave the structural cause in place. A prompt that forbids invention, while the schema still requires a string, asks the model to do two things that cannot both be done. A validation-retry loop is the right tool for format errors and arithmetic inconsistencies, but retries cannot create information that is missing from the source. A self-rated confidence field does not stop invented values, and it depends on calibration that the model does not reliably provide. Even after the schema fix, semantic validation of values is still necessary, because structured output constrains format, not truth.

See Structured outputs for the supported schema subset and nullable types, Strict tool use for how strict: true differs from a plain input schema, and Tool use overview for the documented warning about inferred parameter values.

QUESTION: When the system finds conflicting values, it outputs a discrepancy flag. Every flag passes schema validation, but the flag content varies: "location" is sometimes a page reference and sometimes a paraphrase, and "suggested_resolution" ranges from a concrete correction to "verify this". Detailed field descriptions in the prompt have not helped. What change most reliably produces consistent flags?
answers: Retry each extraction up to three times and keep the response whose flags look most complete.
Ask the model to rate its confidence in each flag so downstream steps can discard vaguely written ones.
Rewrite the field descriptions with stronger wording that every flag must follow the specification exactly.
Add two to four few-shot examples of complete flags showing the exact expected content for each field.
feedbacks: Retries fix format or structural errors that validation can detect, and these flags already pass validation. Repeating the same prompt, which does not specify enough, produces more versions of the same inconsistency. Choosing among them by how complete they look adds cost without fixing the cause.

Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated. It measures how strongly the model believes in the discrepancy, not whether the flag follows the required conventions. Filtering by confidence throws away findings that may be real, and the flags that remain are still inconsistent.

Stronger wording adds emphasis but no new practical detail. The model already has descriptions and still interprets them differently from run to run. A text description of what a field should contain cannot show the convention as clearly as an example of a correctly written flag.

When detailed text descriptions still produce varying output, concrete examples are the most effective way to make format and content conventions consistent. A small set of realistic flags shows what a page reference looks like and what a concrete resolution looks like. This gives the model a pattern that it can match and apply to new documents.
prompt.explanation:
This situation shows the difference between two reliability mechanisms. The JSON schema guarantees the shape of each flag: the fields exist, the types are right, and the JSON parses. It says nothing about whether the content in those fields follows the team's conventions. That is why every flag validates, while reviewers still see a page number in one flag and a loose paraphrase in the next. Problems with content conventions are a prompting problem, not a schema problem.

Anthropic's prompting guidance names few-shot examples as one of the most reliable ways to control output format, tone, and structure. The consistency guide notes that examples of the desired output work better than abstract instructions. An example carries information that a text description cannot. A description like "location should identify where the discrepancy appears" can be interpreted in different ways. A sample flag containing "page 3, Line Items table, row 4" shows the convention directly. Use two to four examples that match real documents. They should cover the ambiguous cases: a discrepancy inside a table versus one in narrative text, and a resolution that is a specific correction versus one that needs human review. Wrap them in an <example> XML tag. The model then has something to match and generalize from, instead of something to interpret again. Examples add to the explicit field descriptions. They do not replace them, and the prompt should still state the format clearly.

The other approaches miss the cause. Rewriting the descriptions with stronger wording adds emphasis without adding any practical detail, so each run still fills the gaps in a different way. Retrying with the same prompt and keeping the response that looks most complete only samples the same variation several times. Retries help when validation can name a specific error to fix, and in this scenario validation passes. Asking the model to rate its own confidence measures something completely different (belief in the discrepancy, not whether the format was followed). It also throws away real findings, while the flags that remain are still inconsistent.

Read the official guidance on examples in Claude prompting best practices and the format-and-example recommendations in Increase output consistency.

QUESTION: The system submitted 5,000 documents as one overnight batch. Results show 4,900 succeeded, while 100 errored with "invalid_request_error" because those documents exceeded the model's context limit. What is the best way to recover the failed extractions?
answers: Retry only the failed documents through synchronous calls with a larger "max_tokens" value so they fit.
Locate the failed documents by their line position in the results file and resubmit them unchanged.
Collect the errored "custom_id" values, split those documents into chunks, and submit only them in a new batch.
Resubmit the entire original batch unchanged so the failed documents get another processing attempt.
feedbacks: The max_tokens parameter limits the model's output, not the size of the input prompt. Raising it does nothing for documents whose input exceeds the context limit. Moving to synchronous calls also gives up the batch discount, and it still does not solve the problem of oversized documents.

Batch results are not guaranteed to come back in the same order as the requests. So line position is not a reliable way to match a result to its document. Even if the documents were identified correctly, resubmitting the oversized documents unchanged would cause the same invalid_request_error again.

Each request in a batch is processed independently, and its result is matched to the source document by custom_id. So the 100 failures can be separated without touching the 4,900 successful results. The error type is invalid_request_error caused by oversized input, so the request payload must be changed before it is sent again. Splitting the documents into chunks is the appropriate change.

An invalid_request_error means the request body itself is the problem. Sending it again unchanged will fail again for the same reason. Rerunning the whole batch also wastes money on 4,900 documents that already produced valid results.
prompt.explanation:
The Message Batches API treats every request in a batch as an independent unit of work. Each request has a custom_id that the developer provides. Each line of the .jsonl results file reports a result.type of succeeded, errored, canceled, or expired for exactly one of those ids. This independence is part of the design tradeoff that makes batches cheap and asynchronous. Requests share no state, so one failure cannot affect the requests around it. The only thing that links a result back to a source document is the id you chose. So recovery is a set operation. Parse the results, divide the ids into groups by outcome, and act only on the groups that need work.

What you do with a failed group depends on the error. Anthropic's own guidance separates an invalid_request_error, where the request body must be fixed before it is sent again, from server-side errors that can be retried as they are. A document that exceeds the context limit clearly belongs in the first category. The request is structurally too large. So the fix is to change the payload: split the document into chunks, give each chunk its own custom_id, and create a new batch that contains only those changed requests. You cannot edit a batch after it is submitted. That is why recovery always means a new batch, not a change to the old one.

Each of the other approaches misses one half of this process. Resubmitting the full batch unchanged repeats an error that is deterministic, and it charges again for 4,900 documents that already produced valid output. Raising max_tokens confuses the output budget with the input size. The document exceeded the context limit, not the response. Using line position in the results file ignores the documented fact that results are not returned in request order, and that is the reason custom_id exists. For future runs, the Token Count API can estimate the size of each request before submission. Then oversized documents are split into chunks in advance, instead of being discovered after a 24-hour window.

See Batch processing and the Retrieve Message Batch results reference for the result format and retry guidance.
